c:Albania: Country in Southeast Europe. Several colonies were founded by the Ancient Greeks along the Albanian coast, most notably Apollonia.
c:Algeria: Country in North Africa. Spanning over 2,381,741 square kilometres (919,595 sq mi), it is the largest country in Africa and the tenth largest in the world.
c:Andorra: Microstate in Southern Europe. Andorra is the sixth-smallest state in Europe and the largest of the European microstates, with an area of 468 square kilometres (181 sq mi) and an estimated population of 90,021 as of July 2026.
c:Angola: Country in Southern Africa. It is the second-largest Portuguese-speaking (Lusophone) country after Brazil in both total area and population and is the seventh-largest country in Africa.
Country in the Lesser Antilles. Antigua and Barbuda has a total area of 440 km2 (170 sq mi), making it one of the smallest countries in the Caribbean.
c:Argentina: Country in South America. It covers an area of 2,780,085 km2 (1,073,397 mi2), making it the second-largest country in South America after Brazil, the fourth-largest country in the Americas, and the eighth-largest country in the world.
c:Armenia: Country in West Asia. The first Armenian state of Urartu was established in 860 BC, and by the 6th century BC it was replaced by the Satrapy of Armenia.
c:Australia: Country in Oceania. It has a land area of 7,688,287 km2 (2,968,464 sq mi), making it the sixth-largest country in the world, and is the world's flattest and driest inhabited continent.
c:Austria: Country in Central Europe. Austria as a state emerged from the remnants of the Eastern and Hungarian March at the end of the first millennium, first as a frontier march of the Holy Roman Empire.
c:Azerbaijan: Country in Eastern Europe and West Asia. Until the 19th century, it remained part of Qajar Iran, but the Russo-Persian wars of 1804–1813 and 1826–1828 forced the Qajar Empire to cede its Caucasian territories to the Russian Empire; the treaties of Gulistan in 1813 and Turkmenchay in 1828 defined the border between Russia and Iran.
c:Bahamas: Country of islands in the Caribbean. Christopher Columbus was the first European to see the islands, making his first landfall in the New World in 1492 when he landed on the island of San Salvador (which the Lucayans called Guanahaní). Later, the Kingdom of Spain shipped the native Lucayans to Hispaniola and enslaved them there.
c:Bahrain: Country in West Asia. The population is 1,588,670 as of 2024, of whom 739,736 (46.6% of the population) are Bahraini nationals, and 848,934 are expatriates (53.4% of the population). Bahrain spans some 760 square kilometres (290 sq mi) and is the third-smallest nation in Asia after Maldives and Singapore.
c:Bangladesh: Country in South Asia. It is the eighth-most populous country in the world with a population of almost 177.8 million people within an area of 148,461 square kilometres (57,321 sq mi). Bangladesh shares land borders with India to the north, west, and east, and Myanmar to the southeast.
c:Barbados: Island nation in the Atlantic Ocean. An English ship, the Olive Blossom, arrived in Barbados on 14 May 1625; its men took possession of the island in the name of King James I. In 1627, the first permanent settlers arrived from England, and Barbados became an English and later British colony.
c:Belarus: Country in Eastern Europe. Around 1300 these lands came fully under the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and subsequently by the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth; this period lasted for 500 years until the 1792–1795 partitions of Poland-Lithuania placed Belarus within the Russian Empire for the first time.
c:Belgium: Country in Northwestern Europe. Belgium covers an area of 30,689 km2 (11,849 sq mi) and has a population of more than 11.8 million; its population density of 383/km2 (990/sq mi) ranks 22nd in the world and sixth in Europe.
c:Belize: Country in Central America. Spain and Britain both laid claim to the land until the British victory over the Spanish in the Battle of St. George's Caye (1798). It became a British colony in 1840, and a Crown colony in 1862.
c:Benin: Country in West Africa. A self-described Marxist–Leninist state called the People's Republic of Benin existed between 1975 and 1990.
c:Bhutan: Country in South Asia. With a population of over 800,000 (800,871) and a territory of 38,394 square kilometres (14,824 sq mi), Bhutan ranks 133rd in land area and 160th in population.
c:Bolivia: Country in South America. While most population and urban centers lie in the Andean region, the largest city and principal industrial center is Santa Cruz de la Sierra, located in the eastern tropical lowlands.
Country in Southeast Europe. Most of modern Bosnia was incorporated into the Roman province of Dalmatia by the mid-first century BCE.
c:Botswana: Country in Southern Africa. Its total area is 581,730 square kilometres (224,610 sq mi). Gaborone, in the South-East District, is the country's capital and largest city.
c:Brazil: Country in South America. Bounded by the Atlantic Ocean on the east, Brazil has a coastline of 7,491 kilometers (4,655 mi), among the longest in the world.
c:Brunei: Country in Southeast Asia. As of 2025, the country had a population of 466,330, being the least populated country in Asia of whom approximately 64,409 resided in the capital and largest city of Bandar Seri Begawan.
c:Bulgaria: Country in Southeastern Europe. It covers a territory of 110,994 square kilometres (42,855 sq mi), making it the tenth largest within the European Union and the sixteenth-largest country in Europe by area.
c:Burkina Faso: Country in West Africa. In 1896, it was colonized by the French as part of French West Africa; in 1958, Upper Volta became a self-governing colony within the French Community.
c:Burundi: Country in East Africa. After the First World War and Germany's defeat, the League of Nations mandated the territories of Burundi and Rwanda to Belgium in a combined territory called Ruanda-Urundi.
c:Cabo Verde: Island country in West Africa. It consists of ten volcanic islands with a combined land area of about 4,033 square kilometres (1,557 sq mi). These islands lie between 600 and 850 kilometres (370 and 530 miles) west of Cap-Vert (i.e., Dakar), the westernmost point of continental Africa, after which they are named.
c:Cambodia: Country in Southeast Asia. It spans an area of about 181,035 km2 (69,898 sq mi), dominated by a low-lying plain and the confluence of the Mekong river and Tonlé Sap, Southeast Asia's largest lake.
c:Cameroon: Country in Central Africa. After World War I, it was divided between France and the United Kingdom as League of Nations mandates until independence in 1960 and 1961 respectively.
c:Canada: Country in North America. Its ten provinces and three territories extend from the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific Ocean and northward into the Arctic Ocean, making it the second-largest country by total area, with the longest coastline of any country.
Country in Central Africa. The CAR covers a land area of about 620,000 square kilometres (240,000 sq mi). As of 2024, it has a population of 5,357,744, consisting of about 80 ethnic groups.
c:Chad: Country in Central Africa. With a total area of around 1,300,000 km2 (500,000 sq mi), Chad is the fifth-largest country in Africa and the twentieth largest nation by area.
c:Chile: Country in South America. The country covers a territorial area of 756,102 square kilometers (291,933 sq mi), sharing borders with Peru to the north, Bolivia to the northeast, Argentina to the east, and the Drake Passage to the south.
c:China: Country in East Asia. It is the world's second-most populous country after India, with a population exceeding 1.4 billion (17% of the world's population). Covering 9.6 million square kilometers (3,700,000 sq mi), it is the third largest country by area.
c:Colombia: Country in South America. It covers an area of 1,141,748 square kilometers (440,831 sq mi) and has a population of around 52 million.
c:Comoros: African island country in the Indian Ocean. Although its population was estimated in 2026 to only number 944,388, the Comoros ranks as one of the most densely populated countries in the world.
c:Congo: Country in Central Africa. It was a Marxist–Leninist state from 1969 to 1992, under the name People's Republic of the Congo (PRC).
c:Costa Rica: Country in Central America. It has a population of around five million in a land area of nearly 51,180 km2 (19,760 sq mi); the capital and largest city is San José, home to around 350,000 residents and two million people in the surrounding metropolitan area.
c:Croatia: Country in Central and Southeast Europe. Settled as two duchies a century later, Croatia was granted independence in 878 under Duke Branimir and elevated into a kingdom under King Tomislav in 925.
c:Cuba: Country in the Caribbean. Cuba is the largest country in the Caribbean by area and the third-largest by population, after Haiti and the Dominican Republic.
c:Cyprus: Island country in the Mediterranean Sea. The island of Cyprus, which is the third largest and third most populous island in the Mediterranean, is divided along the United Nations Buffer Zone between the internationally recognised Republic of Cyprus and the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, which is recognised only by Turkey.
c:Czechia: Country in Central Europe. The Czech Republic has a hilly landscape that covers an area of 78,871 square kilometers (30,452 sq mi) with a mostly temperate continental and oceanic climate.
c:Côte d'Ivoire: Country in West Africa. With 33.2 million inhabitants in 2026, Ivory Coast is the third-most populous country in West Africa after Nigeria and Ghana.
c:Dem. Rep. Congo: Country in Central Africa. With a population of about 124 million people, the Democratic Republic of the Congo is the fourth-most populous country in Africa and the most populous Francophone country in the world.
c:Denmark: Country in northern Europe. Denmark's population is over 6 million (1 May 2025), of which roughly 40% live in Zealand, (Sjælland) the largest and most populated island in Metropolitan Denmark; Copenhagen, (København) the capital and largest city of the Danish Realm, is situated on Zealand and Amager and Slotsholmen.
c:Djibouti: Country in the Horn of Africa. The country has an area of 23,200 km2 (8,958 sq mi). In antiquity, the territory, together with Ethiopia, Eritrea and Somaliland, was part of the Land of Punt.
c:Dominica: Country in the Caribbean. Dominica comprises a land area of 750 km2 (290 sq mi), and the highest point is Morne Diablotins, at 1,448 m (4,751 ft) in elevation.
Island country in the Caribbean. In the Antilles, the country is the second-largest by area after Cuba at 48,671 square kilometers (18,792 sq mi) and the second most populous after Haiti with approximately 11.4 million people in 2024, of whom 3.6 million reside in the metropolitan area of Santo Domingo, the capital city.
c:Ecuador: Country in South America. It also includes the Galápagos Province which contains the Galápagos Islands in the Pacific, about 1,000 kilometers (540 nmi; 620 mi) west of the mainland.
c:Egypt: Country in North Africa. With over 107 million inhabitants, Egypt is the most populous country in the Arab world, third-most populous country in Africa, and 15th-most populated in the world.
c:El Salvador: Country in Central America. Following its independence from Spain in 1821, El Salvador was briefly annexed by the First Mexican Empire before seceding to join the Federal Republic of Central America in 1823.
c:Eq. Guinea: Country in Central Africa. As of 2025, the country has a population of 1,853,559, over 85% of whom are members of the Fang people, the country's dominant ethnic group.
c:Eritrea: Country in the Horn of Africa. The country has a total area of approximately 117,600 km2 (45,406 sq mi), and includes the Dahlak Archipelago and several of the Hanish Islands.
c:Estonia: Country in Northern Europe. The territory of Estonia consists of the mainland, the larger islands of Saaremaa and Hiiumaa, and over 2,300 other islands and islets on the east coast of the Baltic Sea.
c:eSwatini: Country in Southern Africa. At no more than 200 km (120 mi) north to south and 130 km (81 mi) east to west, Eswatini is the second smallest country in continental Africa.
c:Ethiopia: Country in East Africa. Ethiopia covers a land area of 1,104,300 km2 (426,400 sq mi). As of 2026, it has around 138 million inhabitants, making it the 10th-most populous country in the world and 2nd most populous country in Africa.
c:Fiji: Country in Oceania. Fiji consists of an archipelago of more than 330 islands—of which about 110 are permanently inhabited—and more than 500 islets, amounting to a total land area of about 18,300 square kilometres (7,100 sq mi). The most outlying island group is Ono-i-Lau.
c:Finland: Country in Northern Europe. In 1809, as a result of the Finnish War, Finland was captured from Sweden and became an autonomous grand duchy within the Russian Empire.
c:France: Country primarily in Western Europe. Its 18 integral regions—five of which are overseas—span a combined area of 632,702 km2 (244,288 sq mi), with a total population estimated at over 69.1 million in 2026.
c:Gabon: Country in Central Africa. It has an area of 270,000 square kilometres (100,000 sq mi) and a population of 2.6 million people.
c:Gambia: Country in West Africa. The national namesake river demarcates the elongated shape of the country, which has an area of 11,300 square kilometres (4,400 sq mi) and a population of 2,422,712 people at the 1 May 2024 Census which is a 30.45% population increase from 2013.
c:Georgia: Country in Eastern Europe and West Asia. It has a population of 3.9 million, of which over a third live in Tbilisi, the capital and largest city.
c:Germany: Country in Europe. The nation's capital and most populous city is Berlin and its main financial centre is Frankfurt; the largest urban area is the Ruhr.
c:Ghana: Country in West Africa. With over 35 million inhabitants, Ghana is the thirteenth-most populous country in Africa, and the second-most populous country in West Africa.
c:Greece: Country in Southeastern Europe. Greece is considered the cradle of Western civilisation and the birthplace of democracy, Western philosophy, Western literature, historiography, political science, major scientific and mathematical principles, theatre, and the Olympic Games.
c:Grenada: Country in the Caribbean. The southernmost of the Windward Islands, Grenada is directly south of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines and about 100 miles (160 km) north of Trinidad and the South American mainland.
c:Guatemala: Country in Central America. From 1823 to 1841, it was part of the Federal Republic of Central America.
c:Guinea-Bissau: Country in West Africa. Several successful military coups have since interrupted peaceful transfer of power, most recently the 2025 coup, which installed the currently ruling military junta, headed by the transitional president Horta Inta-A Na Man.
c:Guinea: Country in West Africa. At the census held on 1 July 2025, Guinea had a population of over 17.5 million and an area of 245,857 square kilometres (94,926 sq mi). Formerly French Guinea, it achieved independence in 1958.
c:Guyana: Country in South America. With a land area of 214,969 km2 (83,000 sq mi), Guyana is the third-smallest sovereign state by area in mainland South America after Uruguay and Suriname, and is the second-least populous sovereign state in South America after Suriname.
c:Haiti: Country in the Caribbean. The 1791–1804 Haitian Revolution made Haiti the first sovereign state in the Caribbean, the second republic in the Americas, the first country in the Americas to officially abolish slavery, and the only country in history established by a slave revolt.
c:Honduras: Country in Central America. Honduras was home to several important Mesoamerican cultures, most notably the Maya, before Spanish colonization in the 16th century.
c:Hungary: Country in Central Europe. After it was defeated by the Ottoman Empire at the Battle of Mohács in 1526, the kingdom was split into three regions for over 150 years until its reunion under Habsburg rule before the turn of the 18th century.
c:Iceland: Island country in the Atlantic Ocean. Its capital and largest city is Reykjavík, which is home to about 35% of the country's roughly 395,000 residents (excluding nearby towns/suburbs, which are separate municipalities and contribute a further substantial percentage). The official language of the country is Icelandic.
c:India: Country in South Asia. It is the world's seventh-largest country by area and the largest by population.
c:Indonesia: Country in Southeast Asia and Oceania. Comprising between 13,000 and 17,000 islands, including Sumatra, Java, Sulawesi, and parts of Borneo and New Guinea, it is the world's largest archipelagic state and the 14th-largest country by area.
c:Iran: Country in West Asia. Home to one of the world's oldest continuous major civilizations, the territory of present-day Iran was first unified under the Medes in the 7th century BC and reached its territorial height in the 6th century BC, when Cyrus the Great founded the Achaemenid Empire.
c:Iraq: Country in West Asia. The country covers an area of 438,317 square kilometres (169,235 sq mi) and has a population of over 46 million, making it the 58th largest country by area and the 31st most populous in the world.
c:Ireland: Country in Northwestern Europe. The sovereign state shares its only land border with Northern Ireland, which is part of the United Kingdom.
c:Israel: Country in West Asia. The Land of Israel, also called Palestine or the Holy Land, was home to the ancient Canaanites and later the kingdoms of Israel and Judah and Hasmonean Judea.
c:Italy: Country in Southern and Western Europe. It is the tenth-largest country in Europe by area, covering 301,340 km2 (116,350 sq mi), and the third-most populous member state of the European Union, with nearly 59 million inhabitants.
c:Jamaica: Caribbean nation. Jamaica lies about 145 km (78 nmi) south of Cuba, 191 km (103 nmi) west of Hispaniola (the island containing Haiti and the Dominican Republic), and 215 km (116 nmi) southeast of the Cayman Islands (a British Overseas Territory). With 2.8 million people.
c:Japan: Country in East Asia. With a population of almost 123 million as of 2026, it is the world's 11th most populous country.
c:Jordan: Country in West Asia. Following the 1916 Great Arab Revolt during World War I, former Ottoman Syria was partitioned, leading to the establishment of the Emirate of Transjordan in 1921, which became a British protectorate.
c:Kazakhstan: Country in Eastern Europe and Central Asia. The capital is Astana, and the country's largest city and principal cultural and economic center is Almaty, which served as the capital until 1997.
c:Kenya: Country in East Africa. With an estimated population of more than 54.2 million as of mid-2026, it is the 26th-most populous country in the world and the seventh-most populous in Africa.
c:Kiribati: Island country in the central Pacific. The International Date Line goes around Kiribati and swings far to the east, almost reaching 150°W. This brings Kiribati's easternmost islands, the southern Line Islands south of Hawaii, into the same day as the Gilbert Islands and places them in the most advanced time zone on Earth: UTC+14.
c:Kosovo: Country in Southeast Europe. Kosovo has a varied terrain, with high plains along with rolling hills and mountains, some of which have an altitude over 2,500 m (8,200 ft). Its climate is mainly continental with some Mediterranean and Alpine influences.
c:Kuwait: Country in West Asia. In the early 18th century, the territory of modern-day Kuwait was under the jurisdiction of the Bani Khalid clan; then the territory became known as the Sheikdom of Kuwait in 1752 and a British protectorate in 1899.
c:Kyrgyzstan: Country in Central Asia. The capital and largest city is Bishkek which lies on the northern border with Kazakhstan.
c:Laos: Country in Southeast Asia. It has three UNESCO World Heritage Sites: the town of Luang Prabang, the temple complex of Vat Phou, and the Plain of Jars.
c:Latvia: Country in Northern Europe. Russians are the most prominent minority in the country, at almost a quarter of the population; 37.7% of the population speak Russian as their native tongue.
c:Lebanon: Country in West Asia. Lebanon has a population of more than five million and an area of 10,452 square kilometres (4,036 sq mi). Beirut is the country's capital and largest city.
c:Lesotho: Country in Southern Africa. Lesotho was formed in 1824 by King Moshoeshoe I. Continuous encroachments by Dutch settlers made the King enter into an agreement with the United Kingdom to become a protectorate in 1868 and, in 1884, a crown colony.
c:Liberia: Country in West Africa. Between 1822 and the outbreak of the American Civil War in 1861, more than 15,000 freed and free-born African Americans, along with 3,198 Afro-Caribbeans, relocated to Liberia.
c:Libya: Country in North Africa. With an area of almost 1.8 million km2 (700,000 sq mi), Libya is the fourth-largest country in Africa and the Arab world, and the 16th-largest in the world.
c:Liechtenstein: Microstate in Central Europe. Formed in 1719, Liechtenstein became fully independent upon the dissolution of the German Confederation in 1866.
c:Lithuania: Country in Northern Europe. The two realms were united into the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1569, forming one of the largest and most prosperous states in Europe.
c:Luxembourg: Country in Western Europe. In 2026, it had a population of 693,916, which makes it one of the least-populated countries in Europe, albeit with the highest population growth rate; foreign nationals account for almost half the population.
c:Macedonia: Country in Southeast Europe. Skopje, the capital and largest city, is home to a quarter of the country's population of over 1.83 million.
c:Madagascar: African island country in the Indian Ocean. Madagascar was first permanently settled during or before the mid-first millennium CE (roughly 500 to 700) by Austronesian peoples, presumably arriving on outrigger canoes from present-day Indonesia.
c:Malawi: Country in Southeastern Africa. Malawi spans over 118,484 km2 (45,747 sq mi) and has a population of 22,224,282 (as of July 2025). Lilongwe is its capital and largest city.
c:Malaysia: Country in Southeast Asia. A federal constitutional monarchy, it consists of 13 states and three federal territories, separated by the South China Sea into two regions: Peninsular Malaysia on Mainland Southeast Asia and East Malaysia on the island of Borneo.
c:Maldives: Island country in South Asia. With a population of 515,132 in the 2022 census, it is the second least populous country in Asia and the ninth-smallest country by area, but also one of the most densely populated countries.
c:Mali: Country in West Africa. It is the eighth-largest country in Africa and the 23rd largest country in the world, with an area of 1,240,192 square kilometres (478,841 sq mi). It is bordered to the north by Algeria, to the east by Niger, to the northwest by Mauritania, to the south by Burkina Faso and Ivory Coast.
c:Malta: Mediterranean island country. Malta is the world's tenth-smallest country by area, the ninth-most densely populated, and the 166th most populated.
Island country in the Pacific Ocean. The capital and largest city is Majuro, home to approximately half of the country's population.
c:Mauritania: Country in West Africa. By land area Mauritania is the 11th-largest country in Africa and the 28th-largest in the world; 90% of its territory is in the Sahara desert.
c:Mauritius: Island country in the Indian Ocean. The country spans 2,040 square kilometres (790 sq mi) and has an exclusive economic zone covering approximately 580,000 square nautical miles.
c:Mexico: Country in North America. With a population exceeding 134 million as of 2026, Mexico is the tenth-most populous country in the world and is home to the largest number of native Spanish speakers.
c:Micronesia: Island country in Oceania. The federation encompasses the majority of the Caroline Islands (excluding Palau) and consists of four states—from west to east: Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei, and Kosrae—that span the western Pacific just north of the equator for a longitudinal distance of almost 2,700 km (1,700 mi). Together.
c:Moldova: Country in Eastern Europe. Most of Moldovan territory was a part of the Principality of Moldavia from the 14th century until 1812, when it was ceded to the Russian Empire by the Ottoman Empire (to which Moldavia was a vassal state) and became known as Bessarabia.
c:Monaco: Microstate in Western Europe. With a population of 38,423 living in an area of 2.08 km2 (0.80 sq mi), Monaco is the second smallest sovereign state in the world, after Vatican City, as well as the most densely populated.
c:Mongolia: Country in East Asia. It is bordered by Russia to the north and China to the south and covers an area of 1,564,116 square kilometers (603,909 square miles), making it the 18th-largest country in the world and the second largest landlocked nation after Kazakhstan.
c:Montenegro: Country in Southeast Europe. Before the arrival of the Slav peoples in the Balkans in the 6th and 7th centuries CE, the area now known as Montenegro was inhabited principally by people known as Illyrians.
c:Morocco: Country in North Africa. The Moroccan state traces its origins to the establishment of the Idrisid dynasty by Idris I in 788, although its historical territories did not coincide with those of present-day Morocco; the country is regarded as one of the world's oldest continuously existing states.
c:Mozambique: Country in Southeastern Africa. The voyage of Vasco da Gama in 1498 marked the arrival of the Portuguese, who began a gradual process of colonisation and settlement in 1505.
c:Myanmar: Country in Southeast Asia. The country's capital city is Naypyidaw, while its largest city is Yangon (formerly Rangoon). Early civilisations in the area included the Tibeto-Burman-speaking Pyu city-states in Upper Myanmar and the Mon kingdoms in Lower Myanmar.
c:Namibia: Country in Southern Africa. In 1884, the German Empire established rule over most of the territory, forming a colony known as German South West Africa.
c:Nauru: Island country in Oceania. With an area of only 21 square kilometres (8.1 mi2; 2,100 ha; 5,200 acres), Nauru is the third-smallest country in the world, as well as the smallest member state of the Commonwealth of Nations by both area and population.
c:Nepal: Country in South Asia. Nepal has a diverse geography, including fertile plains, subalpine forested hills, and eight of the world's ten highest mountains, including Mount Everest, the highest point above mean sea level on Earth.
c:Netherlands: Country in Northwestern Europe and the Caribbean. In the Republican period, the Dutch Republic experienced major political, economic, and cultural development; this period is commonly known as the Dutch Golden Age.
c:New Zealand: Island country in the Pacific Ocean. In 1642, the Dutch explorer Abel Tasman became the first European to sight and record New Zealand.
c:Nicaragua: Country in Central America. Nicaragua's largest city and national capital is Managua, which is also the fourth-largest city in Central America, with a population of 1,055,247 as of December 2020.
c:Niger: Country in West Africa. It covers a land area of almost 1.27 million km2 (490,000 mi2), making it the sixth-largest country in Africa and the second-largest landlocked nation in Africa behind Chad.
c:Nigeria: Country in West Africa. It covers an area of 923,769 square kilometres (356,669 mi2). With a population of more than 242 million, it is the most populous country in Africa, and the world's sixth-most populous country.
c:North Korea: Country in East Asia. Following the unification of the Three Kingdoms of Korea into Silla and Balhae in the late 7th century, Korea was ruled by the Goryeo dynasty (918–1392) and the Joseon dynasty (1392–1897). The succeeding Korean Empire (1897–1910) was annexed in 1910 into Japan.
c:Norway: Country in northern Europe. Norway has a population of approximately 5.6 million, and a total area of 385,207 square kilometres (148,729 sq mi). Its capital and largest city is Oslo.
c:Oman: Country in West Asia. With an area of 315,331 km2 (121,750 sq mi) and a population of approximately 5.46 million, Oman is the third-largest country on the Arabian Peninsula.
c:Pakistan: Country in South Asia. It is the fifth-most populous country, with a population of over 241.5 million, having the second-largest Muslim population in the world as of 2023.
c:Palau: Country in the Western Pacific. The most populous island is Koror, home to the country's most populous city of the same name.
c:Palestine: Country in West Asia. Gaza was its largest city prior to Israel's forced evacuations in 2023.
c:Panama: Country in Central America. With the backing of the United States, Panama seceded from Colombia in 1903, allowing the construction of the Panama Canal to be completed by the United States Army Corps of Engineers between 1904 and 1914.
c:Papua New Guinea: Country in Oceania. The eastern half of New Guinea was divided in 1884 between German New Guinea in the north and British New Guinea in the south, with the latter ceded to Australia in 1902 and reorganised as the Territory of Papua.
c:Paraguay: Country in South America. The city of Asunción was founded in 1537 as the first capital of the Governorate of the Río de la Plata within the Spanish Empire.
c:Peru: Country in South America. At 1,285,216 km2 (496,225 sq mi), Peru is the 19th largest country in the world, and the third largest in South America.
c:Philippines: Archipelagic country in Southeast Asia. Located in the western Pacific Ocean, it consists of about 7,641 islands, with a total area of about 300,000 square kilometers.
c:Poland: Country in Central Europe. Poland is composed of sixteen voivodeships and is the fifth most populous member state of the European Union (EU), with over 38 million people, and the fifth largest EU country by land area, covering 312,696 km2 (120,733 sq mi). The capital and largest city is Warsaw.
c:Portugal: Country in Southwestern Europe. As a result of the Reconquista against them, Portugal was established as a county of the Kingdom of León in 868 and formally as a kingdom in 1179.
c:Qatar: Country in West Asia. Following Ottoman rule, Qatar became a British protectorate in 1916 and gained independence in 1971.
c:Romania: Country in Southeast and Central Europe. It is the twelfth-largest country in Europe by area, covering 238,397 km2 (92,046 mi2), and the sixth-most populous member state of the European Union, with 19 million inhabitants.
c:Russia: Country in Eastern Europe and North Asia. With a population of over 140 million, Russia is the most populous country in Europe and the ninth-most populous in the world.
c:Rwanda: Country in East Africa. With a population of about 14 million people living within a total area of 26,338 square kilometres (10,169 sq mi), of which land accounts for about 93.7%, Rwanda is the 21st most densely populated country in the world.
c:S. Sudan: Country in East Africa. Following the First Sudanese Civil War, the Southern Sudan Autonomous Region was formed in 1972 and lasted until 1983.
c:Saint Lucia: Country in the West Indies in the eastern Caribbean Sea. The first proven inhabitants of the island, the Arawaks, are believed to have been the first to settle on the island in 200–400 AD.
c:Samoa: Island country in the Pacific Ocean. Because of the Samoans' seafaring skills, pre-20th-century European explorers referred to the entire island group, including American Samoa, as the "Navigator Islands". The country became a colony of the German Empire in 1899 after the Tripartite Convention, and was known as German Samoa.
c:San Marino: Microstate in Southern Europe. San Marino is the fifth-smallest country in the world, with a land area of just over 61 square kilometres (24 sq mi) and a population of 34,042 as of 2025 which in 2026 dropped to 33,559.
c:Saudi Arabia: Country in West Asia. Covering a land area of approximately 2,149,690 km2 (830,000 sq mi), it is the fifth-largest country in Asia and the twelfth-largest in the world.
c:Senegal: Country in West Africa. The state is a semi-presidential republic; since the country's foundation in 1960, it has been recognized as one of the most stable countries on the African continent.
c:Serbia: Country in Southeast and Central Europe. The Serbian Kingdom was established in 1217, reaching its territorial apex in 1346 as the Serbian Empire.
c:Seychelles: Island country in the Indian Ocean. Seychelles is the smallest country in Africa as well as the least populated sovereign African country, with an estimated population of 100,600 in 2022.
c:Sierra Leone: Country in West Africa. Sierra Leone's current territorial configuration was established in two phases: in 1808, the coastal Sierra Leone Colony was founded as part of the British Empire, to be a place to resettle returning Africans after the abolition of the slave trade; then in 1896.
c:Singapore: Island country in Southeast Asia. During World War II, Singapore was occupied by Japan in 1942 and returned to Britain as a Crown colony following Japan's surrender in 1945.
c:Slovakia: Country in Central Europe. In 1241 and 1242, after the Mongol invasion of Europe, much of the territory was destroyed, but was recovered largely thanks to Hungarian king Béla IV.
c:Slovenia: Country in Central Europe. The country is mostly mountainous and forested, covering 20,271 square kilometres (7,827 sq mi). Its population is approximately 2.1 million people.
Island country in Melanesia. In 1568, the Spanish navigator Álvaro de Mendaña was the first European to visit them.
c:Somalia: Country in East Africa. Somalia has an estimated population over 19 million, of which 2.7 million live in the capital and largest city, Mogadishu.
c:South Africa: Country in Southern Africa. Covering an area of 1,221,037 square kilometres (471,445 square miles), the country has a population of over 63 million people, making it the sixth-most populated country in Africa, and 24th-most in the world.
c:South Korea: Country in East Asia. The lattermost eventually unified most of the peninsula for the first time in the late seventh century AD, while Balhae succeeded Goguryeo in the north.
c:Spain: Country in Southern and Western Europe. Featuring the southernmost point of continental Europe, it is the largest country in Southern Europe and the fourth-most populous European Union (EU) member state.
c:Sri Lanka: Country in South Asia. Its executive and judicial capital is Colombo, which is also its largest city and the political, financial and cultural centre of the country; neighboring Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte is the legislative capital.
c:St. Kitts and Nevis: Country in the West Indies. With 261 square kilometres (101 sq mi) of territory, and roughly 48,000 inhabitants, it is the smallest sovereign state in the Western Hemisphere, in both area and population, as well as the world's smallest sovereign Federation.
Archipelagic country in the Caribbean. Spanning a land area of 389 km2 (150 sq mi), most of its territory consists of the northernmost island of Saint Vincent, which includes the capital and largest city, Kingstown.
c:Sudan: Country in Northeast Africa. Sudan has a population of 51.8 million people as of 2025 and occupies 1,886,068 square kilometres (728,215 square miles), making it Africa's third-largest country by area.
c:Suriname: Country in South America. It is the smallest sovereign country in South America by both population and territory, with around 612,985 inhabitants in 2021 in an area of approximately 165,940 square kilometres (64,070 square miles). The capital and largest city is Paramaribo, which is home to roughly half the population.
c:Sweden: Country in northern Europe. At 450,295 square kilometres (173,860 sq mi) and with a population of 10.6 million, Sweden is the largest and most populous Nordic country, and is the fifth-largest country in Europe.
c:Switzerland: Country in Central Europe. Switzerland is geographically divided among the Swiss Alps, the Swiss Plateau, and the Jura Mountains; the Alps cover most of the country's territory, whereas the majority of its 9 million people are concentrated on the plateau, which hosts many of the largest cities and economic centres.
c:Syria: Country in West Asia. With a population of 26 million across an area of 185,180 square kilometres (71,500 sq mi), it is the 56th-most populous and 87th-largest country.
c:São Tomé and Principe: Island country in Central Africa. With a population of 201,800 (2018 official estimate), São Tomé and Príncipe is the second-smallest and second-least populous African sovereign state after Seychelles.
c:Taiwan: Country in East Asia. The combined territories under ROC control consist of 168 islands in total covering 36,193 square kilometers (13,974 square miles). The largest metropolitan area is formed by Taipei (the capital), New Taipei City, and Keelung.
c:Tajikistan: Landlocked country in Central Asia. Within the Soviet Union, the country's borders were drawn when it was part of Uzbekistan as an autonomous republic, before becoming a constituent republic of the Soviet Union on 5 December 1929.
c:Tanzania: Country in East Africa. According to a 2024 estimate, Tanzania has a population of around 67.5 million, making it the most populous African country located entirely south of the equator.
c:Thailand: Country in Southeast Asia. Thailand has a population of nearly 66 million people and covers an area of approximately 513,115 km2 (198,115 sq mi). The capital and largest city is Bangkok.
c:Timor-Leste: Country in Southeast Asia. Resistance continued throughout Indonesian rule and in 1999, a United Nations–sponsored act of self-determination led Indonesia to relinquish control of the territory.
c:Togo: Country in West Africa. Between the 16th and 18th centuries, the coastal region served primarily as a European slave trading outpost, earning Togo and the surrounding region the name "The Slave Coast". In 1884, during the scramble for Africa, Germany established a protectorate in the region called Togoland.
c:Tonga: Country in Oceania. As of September 2026, Tonga has a population of 103,291, 70% of whom live on the main island, Tongatapu.
c:Trinidad and Tobago: Country in the Caribbean. The capital city is Port of Spain, while its largest and most populous municipality is Chaguanas.
c:Tunisia: Country in North Africa. Known for its ancient architecture, souks, and blue coasts, it covers 163,610 km2 (63,170 sq mi), and has a population of 12.1 million.
c:Turkey: Country in Southeastern Europe and West Asia. Turkey is home to over 86 million people; most are ethnic Turks, while Kurds are the largest ethnic minority.
c:Turkmenistan: Country in Central Asia. With over 7 million people, Turkmenistan is the 35th most-populous country in Asia and has the lowest population of the Central Asian republics while being one of the most sparsely populated nations located on the Asian continent.
c:Uganda: Country in East Africa. As of 2024, it had a population of 45.9 million, of whom 1.8 million live in the capital and largest city, Kampala.
c:Ukraine: Country in Eastern Europe. Kievan Rus' became the largest and most powerful realm in Europe in the 10th and 11th centuries, but gradually disintegrated into rival regional powers before being destroyed by the Mongols in the 13th century.
c:United Arab Emirates: Country in West Asia. The UAE borders Oman to the east and northeast, and Saudi Arabia to the south and southwest.
c:United Kingdom: Country in northwestern Europe. The UK includes the island of Great Britain, the north-eastern part of the island of Ireland, and most of the smaller islands within the British Isles, covering 94,354 square miles (244,376 km2). It shares a land border with the Republic of Ireland and is surrounded by the Atlantic Ocean.
c:United States of America: Country primarily in North America. It is a megadiverse country, with the world's fourth-largest total area and third-largest population, exceeding 341 million.
c:Uruguay: Country in South America. Uruguay covers an area of approximately 176,215 square kilometers (68,037 sq mi). It has a population of almost 3.5 million people, of whom nearly 2 million live in the metropolitan area of its capital and largest city, Montevideo.
c:Uzbekistan: Country in Central Asia. The first recorded settlers in Uzbekistan were Eastern Iranian nomads, known as Scythians, who founded kingdoms in Khwarazm, Sogdiana, and Bactria in the 8th–6th centuries BC, as well as in Fergana and Margiana in the 3rd century BC – 6th century AD.
c:Vanuatu: Country in Oceania. The first Europeans to visit the islands were a Spanish expedition led by Portuguese navigator Fernandes de Queirós, who arrived on the largest island, Espíritu Santo, in 1606.
c:Vatican: Enclaved Holy See's independent city-state. The independent state of Vatican City came into existence in 1929 via the Lateran Treaty between the Holy See and the Kingdom of Italy, which spoke of it as a creation, not as a vestige of the much larger Papal States (756–1870), which had previously encompassed much of Central Italy.
c:Venezuela: Country in South America. In 1811, it became one of the first Spanish American territories to declare independence from the Spanish and to form part of the first federal Republic of Colombia (Gran Colombia). It separated as a fully sovereign country in 1830.
c:Vietnam: Country in Southeast Asia. The Han dynasty annexed northern and central Vietnam, which were subsequently under Chinese rule from 111 BC until the first dynasty emerged in 939.
c:Yemen: Country in West Asia. Covering 455,503 square kilometres (175,871 sq mi), with a coastline of approximately 2,000 kilometres (1,200 mi), Yemen is the second-largest country on the Arabian Peninsula by area and the second-largest by population.
c:Zambia: Country in Southern Africa. Following European expeditions in the eighteenth century, the British Empire began to consolidate control of the area following the 1890 British Ultimatum against the Portuguese, who had claimed the area between Angola and Mozambique in the 1885 Pink Map.
c:Zimbabwe: Country in Southeastern Africa. A country of roughly 17.3 million people per 2026 estimates, Zimbabwe's largest ethnic groups are the Northern Ndebele and Shona, who make up 95% of the population, followed by the other smaller minorities.
da-nang: Centrally-governed city of Vietnam. Da Nang has a Human Development Index of 0.800 (very high), ranking fifth among all municipalities and provinces of Vietnam.
dakar: Capital and the largest city of Senegal. The department of Dakar has a population of 1,278,469, and the population of the Dakar metropolitan area was at 4.0 million in 2023.
dallas: City in Texas, United States. Located in northern Texas, it is the ninth-most populous city in the United States and third-most populous city in Texas, with a population of 1.3 million at the 2020 census.
damascus: Capital city of Syria. First settled in the 3rd millennium BC, it was chosen as the capital of the Umayyad Caliphate from 661 to 750.
danube-delta: River delta in Europe. Occurring where the Danube River empties into the Black Sea, most of the Danube Delta lies in Romania (Tulcea County), with a small part located in Ukraine (Odesa Oblast). Its approximate surface area is 4,152 square kilometres (1,603 square miles), of which 3,446 km2 (1,331 sq mi) is in Romania.
dar-es-salaam: Largest city in Tanzania and capital of Dar es Salaam Region. With a population of over 7 million people, Dar es Salaam is the largest city in East Africa by population and the fifth-largest in Africa.
darwin: Capital city of Northern Territory, Australia. It is the smallest, wettest, and most northerly of the Australian capital cities and serves as the Top End's regional centre.
davao-city: Highly urbanized city in Davao Region, Philippines. The region of Davao is home to Mount Apo, the highest mountain in the Philippines, which is highly visible in most parts of Davao City.
dead-sea: Salt lake in the Levant. It is 304 m (997 ft) deep, which makes it the deepest hypersaline lake in the world.
death-valley: Valley in the Mojave Desert, Eastern California. In the afternoon hours of July 10, 1913, the United States Weather Bureau recorded a temperature of 134 °F (56.7 °C) at Furnace Creek in Death Valley, which stands as the highest ambient air temperature ever recorded on the surface of the Earth.
denali: Highest mountain in North America. Its vertical relief above the surrounding plateaus is one of the greatest on Earth, measuring about 18,000 feet (5,500 meters). With a topographic prominence of 20,156 feet (6,144 m) and a topographic isolation of 4,621.1 miles (7,436.9 km).
denpasar: Capital and largest city of Bali, Indonesia. The Denpasar metropolitan area centred on Denpasar (called Sarbagita) had 2,187,198 residents in end 2024.
denver: Capital of Colorado, U.S.. Officially a consolidated city and county, it is located in the South Platte River valley on the western edge of the High Plains.
detroit: Most populous city in Michigan, United States. It is the 26th-most populous city in the United States and the largest U.S. city on the Canada–United States border, with a population of 639,111 at the 2020 census, and an estimated 2025 population of 649,095, its first population increase since 1950.
dettifoss: Waterfall in Northeast Iceland. It is the second largest waterfall in Iceland in terms of volume discharge (behind the Urriðafoss), having an average water flow of 193 m³/s. The superlative of "most powerful" comes from its water flow multiplied by its fall distance.
dhaka: Capital and largest city of Bangladesh. With an estimated population of 36.6 million, Dhaka is the second largest city by population in the world, and is widely considered to be the most densely populated built-up urban area in the world.
dijon: Prefecture of Bourgogne-Franche-Comté, France. As of 2023, the population of the commune was 161,830, making it the most populous commune in Bourgogne-Franche-Comté.
dili: Capital and largest city of Timor-Leste. The city has served as the economic hub and chief port of what is now Timor-Leste since its designation as the capital of Portuguese Timor in 1769.
djibouti: Capital and largest city in Djibouti. The settlement was founded in 1888 by the French, on land leased from the ruling Somali and Afar Sultans.
dodoma: Capital of Tanzania. With a population of 765,179 as per 2022 which is projected to reach 1,000,000 by the end of 2026 (given the current pace of relocation of government organizations and NGOs), it is also the administrative capital of both Dodoma Municipal Council and the entire Dodoma Region.
doha: Capital and largest city of Qatar. Located on the Persian Gulf coast in the east of the country, north of Al Wakrah and south of Al Khor and Lusail, it is home to most of the country's population.
douala: Largest city and economic capital of Cameroon. It was home to Central Africa's largest port, now being replaced by Kribi port.
drake-passage: Strait connecting the Atlantic, Pacific, and Southern Oceans. Traversing the Drake Passage is considered one of the most treacherous voyages for ships to make.
dresden: Capital city of Saxony, Germany. It is the 12th most populous city of Germany, the fourth largest by area (after Berlin, Hamburg, and Cologne), and the third-most populous city in the area of former East Germany, after Berlin and Leipzig.
dubai: Largest city in the United Arab Emirates. Founded in the early 18th century as a pearling and fishing settlement, Dubai became a regional trade hub in the 20th century after declaring itself a free port (1901) and extending the Creek (1961). Modest oil revenue helped accelerate Dubai's development from the 1960s to the 1990s.
dublin: Capital and largest city of Ireland. Dublin is the largest city by population on the island of Ireland; at the 2022 census, the city council area had a population of 592,713, while the city, including suburbs, had a population of 1,263,219, and County Dublin had a population of 1,501,500.
dubrovnik: Coastal city in southern Croatia. Recognizing its outstanding medieval architecture and fortifications, UNESCO inscribed the Old City of Dubrovnik as a World Heritage Site in 1979.
dunedin: City in Otago, New Zealand. With an estimated population of 132,800 as of June 2025, Dunedin is New Zealand’s seventh most populous metropolitan and urban area.
dunkirk-evacuation: Evacuation of Allied forces in mid-1940. After the Phoney War of October 1939 to April 1940, Germany invaded Belgium, the Netherlands, and France on 10 May 1940.
durban: City in South Africa. Durban is the seat of the larger eThekwini Metropolitan Municipality, which spans an area of 2,556 km2 (987 sq mi) and had a population of 4.2 million in 2022, making the metropolitan population one of Africa's largest on the Indian Ocean.
dushanbe: Capital and largest city of Tajikistan. Until 1929, the city was known in Russian as Dyushambe, and from 1929 to 1961 as Stalinabad, after Joseph Stalin.
dusseldorf: Capital of North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany. It is the second-largest city in the state after Cologne and the sixth-largest city in Germany, with a 2024 population of 618,685.
easter-island: Island in the southeastern Pacific. In 1995, UNESCO named Easter Island a World Heritage Site, with much of the island protected within Rapa Nui National Park.
edinburgh-castle: Historic castle in Edinburgh, Scotland. As one of the most important strongholds in the Kingdom of Scotland, the castle was involved in many historical conflicts from the Wars of Scottish Independence in the 14th century to the Jacobite rising of 1745.
edinburgh: Capital city of Scotland. Edinburgh had a population of 506,520 in 2020, making it the second-most-populous city in Scotland (behind Glasgow) and the seventh-most-populous in the United Kingdom.
edmonton: Capital of Alberta, Canada. Located about 290 kilometres (180 mi) north of Calgary, the city anchors the northern end of what Statistics Canada defines as the "Calgary–Edmonton Corridor". The Edmonton area was first inhabited by First Nations peoples, and was also a historic site for the Métis.
eiffel-tower: Tower in Paris, France. It was designated a monument historique in 1964, and was named part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site ("Paris, Banks of the Seine") in 1991.
el-escorial: Monastery and historical residence of the king of Spain. Built between 1563 and 1584 by order of King Philip II (who reigned 1556–1598), El Escorial is the largest Renaissance building in the world.
ellora-caves: Ancient cave temples in Maharashtra, India. It is one of the largest rock-cut cave complexes in the world, with artwork dating from AD 600–1000, including Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain caves.
empire-state-building: Office skyscraper in Manhattan, New York. As of 2025, the building is the eighth-tallest building in New York City, the tenth-tallest completed skyscraper in the United States, and the 59th-tallest completed skyscraper in the world.
english-channel: Body of water between Great Britain and France. It is the smallest of the shallow seas around the continental shelf of Europe, covering an area of some 75,000 square kilometres (22,000 square nautical miles; 29,000 square miles). The Channel aided the United Kingdom in becoming a naval superpower, serving as a natural defence against invasions.
ephesus: Ancient Greek city in Anatolia. The city was famous in its day for the nearby Temple of Artemis (completed around 550 BC), which has been designated one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.
eruption-of-mount-vesuvius-in-79-ad: Volcanic eruption in Italy. Archaeological excavations have revealed much of the towns and the lives of the inhabitants, leading to the area becoming Vesuvius National Park and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
falklands-war: 1982 undeclared Argentina–United Kingdom war. The conflict began on 2 April 1982 when Argentina invaded the Falkland Islands, followed by the invasion of South Georgia the next day.
fall-of-constantinople: 1453 Ottoman conquest of the Byzantine capital. The walls of Constantinople, especially the Theodosian walls, protected Constantinople from attack for 800 years and were noted as some of the most advanced defensive systems in the world at the time.
fall-of-rome: Loss of political control in antiquity. In 376, a large migration of Goths and other non-Roman people, fleeing from the Huns, entered the Empire.
fall-of-saigon: End of the Vietnam War, 30 April 1975. By the next day, President Minh had surrendered while the PAVN/VC had occupied the important points of the city and raised the VC flag over the South Vietnamese Presidential Palace, ending the existence of South Vietnam and its predecessor (1949–1975). For the first time since 1954.
fall-of-tenochtitlan: 1521 conquest of the Aztec capital by the Spanish Empire and rival indigenous tribes. It occurred in 1521 following extensive negotiations between local factions and Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés.
fall-of-the-berlin-wall: 1989 destruction of the Berlin Wall. The Berlin Wall fell on 9 November 1989 during the Peaceful Revolution, marking the beginning of the destruction of the figurative Iron Curtain, as East Berlin transit restrictions were overwhelmed and discarded.
faro: Municipality in Algarve, Portugal. Faro municipality covers an area of 202.57 km2 (78.21 sq mi) and, as of 2024, had 70,347 inhabitants, making it the second most populous municipality in the Algarve after Loulé.
faroe-islands: Autonomous territory of Denmark. Located between Iceland, Norway, and the Hebrides and Shetland isles of Scotland, the islands have a population of 54,870 as of November 2025 and a land area of 1,393 km2 (538 sq mi). The official language is Faroese, which is partially mutually intelligible with Icelandic.
fenway-park: Baseball stadium in Boston, Massachusetts. While the stadium was built in 1912, it was substantially rebuilt in 1934, and underwent major renovations and modifications in the 21st century.
fez: City in Fez-Meknes, Morocco. It is one of the largest cities in Morocco, with a population of 1.256 million, according to the 2024 census.
first-battle-of-the-marne: First major battle of World War I, 1914. The First Battle of the Marne or known in France as the Miracle on the Marne (French: miracle de la Marne) was a battle of the First World War fought from 5 to 12 September 1914.
florence: Largest city in Tuscany, Italy. The Metropolitan Area of Florence, Prato and Pistoia, constituted in 2000 over an area of roughly 4,800 square kilometres (1,850 sq mi), is home to 1.5 million people.
florianopolis: Capital city of Santa Catarina, Brazil. It has a population of 537,211, according to the 2022 Brazilian census, the second-most populous city in the state (after Joinville), and the 39th in Brazil.
forbidden-city: Imperial palace complex in Beijing, China. The Forbidden City was constructed from 1406 to 1420, and was the imperial palace and winter residence of the Emperor of China from the Ming dynasty (since the Yongle Emperor) to the end of the Qing dynasty, between 1420 and 1924.
fort-knox: United States Army post in Kentucky, United States. The 109,000-acre (170 sq mi; 440 km2) base covers parts of Bullitt, Hardin and Meade counties.
fortaleza: Capital city of Ceará, Brazil. It is Brazil's 4th largest city—Fortaleza surpassed Salvador in 2024 census with a population of slightly over 2.5 million—and 12th among cities with the highest gross domestic product.
frankfurt: Largest city in Hesse, Germany. Its 778,589 inhabitants as of 2025 make it the fifth-most populous city in Germany.
freetown: Capital and largest city of Sierra Leone. The population of Freetown was 1,347,559 as of the 2024 census.
french-revolution: 1789–1799 sociopolitical change in France. Financial crisis and widespread social distress led to the convocation of the Estates General in May 1789, its first meeting since 1614.
frida-kahlo-museum: Art museum in Mexico City. The building was Kahlo's birthplace, the home where she grew up, lived with her husband Diego Rivera for a number of years, and where she later died in a room on the upper floor.
funafuti: Capital of Tuvalu, atoll and district. In 1909, the first resident magistrate was appointed to Funafuti; in 1915, Funafuti, along with the rest of the Ellice Islands, were incorporated into the Gilbert and Ellice Islands as a crown colony.
fushimi-inari-taisha: Shinto shrine near Kyoto, Japan. The shrine was formally founded in 711 CE by the Hata clan, an influential immigrant group from the Korean Peninsula.
gaborone: Capital and largest city of Botswana. Its metropolitan area is home to 534,842 inhabitants at the 2022 census.
galapagos-islands: Ecuadorian volcanic archipelago. The Galápagos Islands (Spanish: Islas Galápagos) are an archipelago of volcanic islands in the Eastern Pacific, located around the equator, 485 nautical miles (898 km; 558 mi) west of the mainland of South America.
gallipoli-campaign: Military campaign during World War I. The Gallipoli campaign, the Dardanelles campaign, the Defence of Gallipoli or the Battle of Gallipoli was a military campaign in the First World War on the Gallipoli Peninsula (now Gelibolu) from 19 February 1915 to 9 January 1916. The Allied powers.
galway: City in Connacht, Ireland. It is the most populous settlement in the province of Connacht, the fifth most populous city on the island of Ireland and the fourth most populous in the Republic of Ireland, with a population at the 2022 census of 85,910.
gateway-arch: US National Historic Landmark in St. Louis, Missouri. Construction began on February 12, 1963, and was completed on October 28, 1965, at an overall cost of $13 million (equivalent to $98.4 million in 2024). The monument opened to the public on June 10, 1967.
gateway-of-india: Landmark monument in Mumbai, India. It was erected to commemorate the landing of King George V of the United Kingdom for his coronation as the Emperor of India in December 1911 at Strand Road near Wellington Fountain.
gdansk: City in Pomeranian Voivodeship, Poland. With a population of 486,492, it is Poland's sixth-largest city and its major seaport.
geirangerfjord: Fjord in Møre og Romsdal, Norway. It is a 15-kilometre-long (9+1⁄2 mi) branch off the Sunnylvsfjorden, which itself is a branch off the Storfjorden (lit. 'Great Fjord'). The small village of Geiranger is located at the end of the fjord where the Geirangelva river empties into it.
geneva: City in Switzerland. Geneva is a global city, an international financial centre, and a worldwide centre for diplomacy, which has led to it being called the "Peace Capital". It hosts the highest number of international organisations in the world.
genoa: Largest city in Liguria, Italy. While its metropolitan city has 820,691 inhabitants, more than 1.5 million people live in the wider metropolitan area stretching along the Italian Riviera.
georgetown-guyana: Capital of Guyana. The city recorded a population of 125,683 as of 2022 census.
gettysburg-address: 1863 speech by Abraham Lincoln. Lincoln delivered the speech on the afternoon of November 19, 1863, during a formal dedication of Soldiers' National Cemetery, now known as Gettysburg National Cemetery, on the grounds where the Battle of Gettysburg had been fought four and a half months earlier, between July 1 and July 3, 1863.
ghent: Capital of East Flanders province, Belgium. With 270,473 inhabitants at the end of 2024, Ghent is Belgium's second largest municipality by number of inhabitants.
giant-s-causeway: Interlocking basalt columns in Northern Ireland. It was declared a World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 1986 and a national nature reserve by the Department of the Environment for Northern Ireland in 1987.
giza-pyramid-complex: Archaeological site near Cairo, Egypt. It forms the northernmost part of the 16,000 ha (160 km2; 62 sq mi) Pyramid Fields of the Memphis and its Necropolis UNESCO World Heritage Site, inscribed in 1979.
giza: City in Greater Cairo, Egypt. Giza is most famous as the location of the Giza Plateau, the site of some of the most impressive ancient monuments in the world, including a complex of ancient Egyptian royal mortuary and sacred structures, among which are the Great Sphinx, the Great Pyramid of Giza.
glacier-bay: National park in Alaska, United States. Glacier Bay became part of a binational UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979, and was inscribed as a Biosphere Reserve in 1986.
glasgow: Largest city in Scotland. More than 1,000,000 people live in the Greater Glasgow urban area, while the wider Glasgow City Region is home to more than 1,800,000 people around a third of Scotland's population.
glorious-revolution: British revolution of 1688. The two ruled as joint monarchs of England, Scotland, and Ireland until Mary's death in 1694, when William became ruler in his own right.
goa: State in Southwest India. Goa became an overseas territory of the Portuguese Empire and part of what was then known as Portuguese India, remaining under Portuguese rule for approximately 451 years until its annexation by India in December 1961.
gobekli-tepe: Neolithic archaeological site in Turkey. It is known for its large circular structures that contain large stone pillars – among the world's oldest known megaliths.
gobi-desert: Desert in East Asia. The Gobi Desert is a large, cold desert and grassland region in southern Mongolia and North China.
golden-gate-bridge: Bridge in the San Francisco Bay Area. Recognized by the American Society of Civil Engineers as one of the Wonders of the Modern World, the bridge is one of the most internationally recognized symbols of San Francisco and California.
golden-temple: Sikh religious site in Punjab, India. The gurdwara complex has been nominated as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and its application is pending on the tentative list of UNESCO.
gothenburg: City in Västergötland, Sweden. Situated by the Kattegat on the west coast of Sweden 400 km from the capital, it is the gubernatorial seat of Västra Götaland County, with a population of approximately 600,000 in the city proper and about 1.1 million inhabitants in the metropolitan area.
graceland: Home of Elvis Presley in Memphis, Tennessee, US. It was opened to the public as a house museum on June 7, 1982; as of 2024, it receives around 600,000 visitors annually, the second most visited home in the United States after the White House.
granada: Municipality in Andalusia, Spain. With a population of 233,532 as of 2024, it is the 20th-largest city in Spain and is an important wine growing region It was the last Muslim stronghold in Islamic Spain.
grand-canyon: Steep-sided canyon in Arizona, US. The Grand Canyon is 277 miles (446 km) long, up to 18 miles (29 km) wide and attains a depth of over a mile (6,093 feet or 1,857 meters). The canyon and adjacent rim are contained within Grand Canyon National Park, the Kaibab National Forest, Grand Canyon–Parashant National Monument.
grand-central-terminal: Railway terminal in Manhattan, New York. It also serves the Long Island Rail Road through Grand Central Madison, a 16-acre (6.5 ha) addition to the station located underneath the Metro-North tracks, built from 2007 to 2023.
grand-palace: Royal residence in Bangkok, Thailand. The palace has been the official residence of the Kings of Siam (and later Thailand) since 1782.
graz: Capital of Styria, Austria. On 1 January 2026, Graz had a population of around 307,912 to 345,391 including residents with a secondary residence.
great-barrier-reef: Coral reef system in Queensland, Australia. The Great Barrier Reef is the world's largest coral reef system, composed of over 2,900 individual reefs and 900 islands stretching for over 2,300 kilometres (1,400 mi) over an area of approximately 344,400 square kilometres (133,000 mi2). The reef is located in the Coral Sea.
great-fire-of-london: 1666 conflagration in England. The Great Fire of London occurred from Sunday 2 September to Wednesday 5 September 1666, gutting the medieval City of London inside the old Roman city wall, while also extending past the wall to the west.
great-mosque-of-djenne: Mosque in Djenné, Mali. Along with the "Old Towns of Djenné", it was designated a World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 1988.
great-rift-valley: Continuous geographic trench from Asia to Southeast Africa. The term was introduced by British geologist John Walter Gregory in 1896, following on from the work of Austrian geologist Eduard Suess, who first proposed the existence of a linked set of features extending from Syria to Mozambique.
great-salt-lake: Salt lake in Utah, United States. In 2021, after years of sustained drought and increased water diversion upstream of the lake, it fell to its lowest recorded area at 950 square miles (2,500 km2), falling below the previous low set in 1963.
great-wall-of-china: Series of fortifications in northern China. Successive dynasties expanded the wall system; the best-known sections were built by the Ming dynasty (1368–1644). To aid in defense, the Great Wall utilized watchtowers, troop barracks, garrison stations, signaling capabilities through the means of smoke or fire.
great-zimbabwe: Ruins of an ancient/medieval city in southeast Zimbabwe. The Zimbabwe state centred on it likely covered 50,000 km² (19,000 sq mi). It is recognised as a World Heritage Site by UNESCO.
grenoble: Prefecture and commune in Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, France. The population of the commune of Grenoble was 156,140 as of 2023, while the population of the Grenoble metropolitan area (French: aire d'attraction de Grenoble) was 727,380 in 2023, which makes it the largest metropolis in the Alps, ahead of Innsbruck and Bolzano.
griffith-observatory: Observatory in Los Angeles, California. Named after its benefactor, Griffith J. Griffith, admission has been free since the observatory's opening in 1935, in accordance with his will.
groningen: City and municipality in the Netherlands. Dubbed the "capital of the north", Groningen is the largest city as well as the economic and cultural centre of the northern part of the country; as of January 2025, it had 244,807 inhabitants.
guadalajara: City and municipality in Jalisco, Mexico. According to the 2020 census, the city has a population of 1,385,629 people, making it the 8th most populous city in Mexico, while the Guadalajara metropolitan area has a population of 5,268,642.
guadalcanal-campaign: U.S. military campaign in World War II. It was fought between 7 August 1942 and 9 February 1943, and involved major land and naval battles on and surrounding the island of Guadalcanal.
guangzhou: Capital of Guangdong, China. Located on the Pearl River, about 120 kilometres (75 mi) northwest of Hong Kong and 145 kilometres (90 mi) north of Macau, Guangzhou has a history of over 2,200 years and was a major terminus of the Silk Road.
guatemala-city: Capital and largest city of Guatemala. The present city was founded by the Spanish after their colonial capital, now called Antigua Guatemala, was destroyed by the devastating 1773 Santa Marta earthquake and its aftershocks.
guayaquil: Most populous city in Ecuador. With a population of 2,746,403 inhabitants, it is the most populous city in the country, the fifth largest in the Andean Community, and the largest non-capital city in South America.
guggenheim-museum-bilbao: Modern and contemporary art museum in Bilbao, Spain. It was inaugurated on 18 October 1997 by King Juan Carlos I of Spain, with an exhibition of 250 contemporary works of art.
gulf-of-mexico: Marginal sea of the Atlantic Ocean. The Gulf of Mexico basin is roughly oval and is about 810 nautical miles (1,500 kilometers; 930 miles) wide.
gulf-war: 1990–1991 conflict in the Middle East. The coalition's efforts were in two phases: Operation Desert Shield, which marked the military buildup from August 1990 to January 1991; and Operation Desert Storm, from the bombing campaign against Iraq on 17 January until the American-led liberation of Kuwait on 28 February.
gullfoss: Waterfall in Bláskógabyggð and Hrunamannahreppur, Iceland. It is one of the most popular tourist attractions in the country, and is included in "Golden Circle" tours of the countryside near Reykjavík.
gyeongbokgung: Palace in Seoul, South Korea. Almost all of its around 500 structures were sold off and shipped elsewhere; by the 1945 liberation of Korea, only 40 pre-colonial buildings remained.
hadrian-s-wall: Defensive fortification in Roman Britain. The largest Roman archaeological feature in Britain, it runs a total of 73 miles (117.5 kilometres). Regarded as a British cultural icon, Hadrian's Wall is one of Britain's major ancient tourist attractions.
hagia-sophia: Mosque and former church in Istanbul, Turkey. It was formerly a church (360–1453) and a museum (1935–2020). The last of three church buildings to be successively erected on the site by the Eastern Roman Empire, it was completed in AD 537, becoming the world's largest interior space and among the first to employ a fully pendentive dome.
haifa: City in Northern Israel. The earliest known settlement in the vicinity was Tell Abu Hawam, a small port city established in the Late Bronze Age (14th century BCE). In the 3rd century CE, Haifa was known as a dye-making center.
halifax: Canadian provincial capital. As of 2024, it is estimated that the population of the Halifax CMA was 530,167, with 348,634 people in its urban area.
halong-bay: Bay in northern Vietnam. Hạ Long Bay has an area of around 1,553 km2 (600 sq mi), including 1,969 islets, most of which are made of limestone.
hamburg: City and state in Germany. Before the 1871 unification of Germany, it was a fully sovereign city state, and before 1919 formed a civic republic headed constitutionally by a class of hereditary Grand Burghers, or Hanseaten.
hampi: Ancient and medieval monuments, a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Karnataka, India. Hampi-Vijayanagara is estimated to be the world's second-largest city by 1500, after Beijing, and probably India's richest at that time, attracting traders from Persia and Portugal.
hangzhou: Capital of Zhejiang Province, China. Established as a county seat in 221 BC, Hangzhou later served as the capital of the Wuyue Kingdom (923–997) and the Southern Song dynasty (1138–1276). The city has three UNESCO World Heritage Sites: the West Lake Cultural Landscape, the Grand Canal, and the Archaeological Ruins of Liangzhu City.
hanoi: Capital and centrally-governed city of Vietnam. Hanoi had the second-highest gross regional domestic product of all Vietnamese provinces and centrally-governed city at US$48 billion in 2023, behind Ho Chi Minh City.
hanover: Capital of Lower Saxony, Germany. Its population of 535,932 (2021) makes it the 13th-largest city in Germany as well as the fourth-largest in northern Germany after Berlin, Hamburg and Bremen.
harare: Capital and largest city of Zimbabwe. Salisbury was thereafter the seat of the Southern Rhodesian (later Rhodesian) government and, between 1953 and 1963, the capital of the Central African Federation.
hassan-ii-mosque: Mosque in Casablanca, Morocco. Its minaret is the world's second tallest minaret at 210 metres (689 ft). Completed in 1993, it was designed by Michel Pinseau under the guidance of King Hassan II and built by Moroccan artisans from all over the kingdom.
havana: Capital and largest city of Cuba. Founded in 1519 by the Spanish Empire, Havana had already overtaken Santiago by the mid-16th century due to the geostrategic advantages of its harbor, becoming the capital of the island in 1552.
hawaii: U.S. state. Hawaii consists of 137 volcanic islands that make up almost the entire Hawaiian archipelago (the exception is Midway Atoll). Spanning 1,500 miles (2,400 km), the state is physiographically and ethnologically part of the Polynesian subregion of Oceania.
hearst-castle: Historical estate in San Simeon, California. Conceived by William Randolph Hearst, the publishing tycoon, and his architect Julia Morgan, the castle was built between 1919 and 1947.
heidelberg: City in Baden-Württemberg, Germany. Heidelberg University, founded in 1386, is Germany's oldest and one of Europe's most reputable universities.
helsinki: Capital and most populous city of Finland. Helsinki, until about 1930 known in English by its Swedish name of Helsingfors, is the capital and most populous city in Finland.
hermitage-museum: Museum in Saint Petersburg, Russia. The Art Newspaper ranked the museum 10th in their list of the most visited art museums, with 2,812,913 visitors in 2022.
himeji-castle: Japanese castle in Hyōgo Prefecture. The fort was dismantled and rebuilt as Himeyama Castle in 1346 and then remodeled into Himeji Castle two centuries later.
hindenburg-disaster: 1937 airship fire in the US. The LZ 129 Hindenburg (Luftschiff Zeppelin #129; Registration: D-LZ 129) was a German commercial passenger-carrying rigid airship, the lead ship of the Hindenburg class, the longest class of flying machine and the largest airship by envelope volume.
hiroshima: City in Chūgoku, Japan. As of June 1, 2019, the city had an estimated population of 1,199,391.
ho-chi-minh-city: Largest city in Vietnam. As the biggest financial centre of Vietnam, Ho Chi Minh City has the largest gross regional domestic product out of all Vietnamese provinces and municipalities, contributing around a quarter of the country's total GDP.
hobart: Capital city of Tasmania, Australia. Its skyline is dominated by the 1,271-metre (4,170 ft) kunanyi / Mount Wellington, and its harbour forms the second-deepest natural port in the world, with much of the city's waterfront consisting of reclaimed land.
hobbiton-movie-set: Movie Set / Tourist Attraction in Waikato, New Zealand. It is situated on a family-run farm about 8 kilometres (5.0 mi) west of Hinuera and 10 kilometres (6.2 mi) southwest of Matamata, in Waikato, New Zealand, and is now a Tolkien tourism destination, offering a guided tour of the set.
hollywood-sign: Landmark in Los Angeles, California. It was originally erected in 1923 as a temporary advertisement for a local real estate development, and spelled out "HOLLYWOODLAND" in 50-foot-tall (15.2 m) white uppercase letters in a word 450 feet (137.2 m) long.
hong-kong: Special administrative region of China. Hong Kong was established as a colony of the British Empire after the Qing dynasty ceded Hong Kong Island in 1841–1842 as a result of losing the First Opium War.
honiara: Capital city in Capital territory, Solomon Islands. As of 2019, it had a population of 129,569 people.
honolulu: Capital and largest city in Hawaii, US. Honolulu has been the capital of Hawaii since 1845, first as seat of the independent Hawaiian Kingdom until the kingdom's overthrow in 1893, then of the U.S. territory established after annexation in 1898, and since 1959 of the state of Hawaii.
hoover-dam: Dam in Nevada and Arizona, US. Constructed between 1931 and 1936, during the Great Depression, it was dedicated on September 30, 1935, by President Franklin D. Roosevelt.
houses-of-parliament: Meeting place of the UK Parliament. The palace has been a Grade I listed building since 1970 and part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987.
houston: Largest city in Texas, United States. Houston was founded by land investors on August 30, 1836, at the confluence of Buffalo Bayou and White Oak Bayou (a point now known as Allen's Landing) and incorporated as a city on June 5, 1837.
hudson-bay: Large body of saltwater in northeastern Canada. The Hudson Bay drainage basin drains a very large area, about 3,861,400 km2 (1,490,900 sq mi), that includes parts of southeastern Nunavut, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Ontario, Quebec, all of Manitoba, and parts of the U.S. states of North Dakota, South Dakota, Minnesota, and Montana.
hyderabad: Capital of Telangana, India. According to the 2011 census of India, Hyderabad is the fourth-most populous city in India, with a population of 6.9 million residents within the city limits and 9.7 million residents in the metropolitan region, making it the sixth-most populous metropolitan area in India.
iguazu-falls: Waterfalls on the Iguazú River on the border of Argentina and Brazil. The falls are protected within Iguazú National Park in Argentina and Iguaçu National Park in Brazil, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1984 and 1986 respectively.
incheon: City in South Korea. Inhabited since the Neolithic, Incheon was home to just 4,700 people when it became an international port in 1883.
independence-hall: Building in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. They founded the Continental Army there on June 14, 1775, and the Declaration of Independence was adopted there on July 4, 1776.
indian-ocean: Oceanic division. The Indian Ocean is the third-largest of the world's five oceanic divisions, covering 70,560,000 km2 (27,240,000 sq mi) or approximately 20% of the water area of Earth's surface.
innsbruck: Capital city of Tyrol, Austria. The city had a population of 132,188 in 2024.
inverness: City in the Highlands of Scotland. A regional hub for healthcare, education and research, business and economic services, public administration, culture, music and entertainment, media, communications, transport and leisure, the city provides a range of services for the wider Highlands and Islands Region.
ipanema: Neighbourhood in Rio de Janeiro, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. The beach at Ipanema became known internationally with the popularity of the bossa nova song, "The Girl from Ipanema" ("Garota de Ipanema"), written by Antônio Carlos Jobim and Vinícius de Moraes.
isfahan: City in Isfahan province, Iran. The city has a population of approximately 2,238,000, making it the third-most populous city in Iran, after Tehran and Mashhad, and the second-largest metropolitan area.
islamabad: Capital of Pakistan. Built as a planned city along the Margalla Hills in the 1960s and established in 1967, Islamabad replaced Karachi as Pakistan's national capital.
istanbul: Largest city in Turkey. Over nearly 16 centuries following its reestablishment as Constantinople in 330 AD, it served as the capital of four empires: the Roman Empire (330–395), the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire (395–1204 and 1261–1453), the Latin Empire (1204–1261), and the Ottoman Empire (1453–1922).
itsukushima-shrine: Shinto shrine in Hiroshima Prefecture, Japan. The shrine complex is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the Japanese government has designated several buildings and possessions as National Treasures.
jaipur: Capital of Rajasthan, India. Located 268 km (167 miles) from the national capital New Delhi, Jaipur is also known as the Pink City due to the dominant colour scheme of its buildings in the old city.
jakarta: Capital and largest city in Indonesia. Jakarta itself covers about 662 square kilometres (256 square miles), but the wider Jakarta metropolitan area—locally known as Jabodetabek—is among the largest urban agglomerations in the world by area.
jeddah: Second-largest city in Saudi Arabia. Jeddah Islamic Port, on the Red Sea, is the thirty-sixth largest seaport in the world and the second-largest and second-busiest seaport in the Middle East.
jemaa-el-fnaa: Moroccan cultural heritage site. It remains the main square of Marrakesh, used by locals and tourists.
