san-juan: Capital and largest city of Puerto Rico. San Juan was founded by Spanish colonists in 1521, who called it Ciudad de Puerto Rico (Spanish for "Rich Port City"). Puerto Rico's capital is the second oldest European-established capital city in the Americas, after Santo Domingo, in the Dominican Republic, founded in 1496.
san-salvador: Capital of El Salvador. The municipality of San Salvador has 525,990 inhabitants (2024). The Metropolitan Area of San Salvador, which comprises the capital itself and 13 of its municipalities, has a population of 2,404,097.
sanaa: Capital and largest city of Yemen. At an elevation of 2,300 metres (7,500 ft), Sanaa is the seventh highest capital city in the world and is situated between the Sarawat Mountains of Jabal An-Nabi Shu'ayb and Jabal Tiyal, considered the highest mountains in the Arabian Peninsula and one of the highest in the Middle East.
santa-cruz-de-la-sierra: Most populous city in Bolivia. The city was first founded in 1561 by Spanish explorer Ñuflo de Chavez about 200 km (124 mi) east of its current location, and was moved several times until it was finally established on the Pirai River in the late 16th century.
santa-fe: Capital city of New Mexico, United States. The county seat of Santa Fe County, Santa Fe is situated at the foothills of the Sangre de Cristo Mountains at the highest altitude of any U.S. state capital, with an elevation of 6,998 feet (2,133 m). Founded in 1610 as the capital of Nuevo México, a province of New Spain.
santiago-bernabeu-stadium: Stadium in Madrid, Spain. Named after former Real Madrid player and president Santiago Bernabéu (1895–1978), the stadium is one of the world's most famous football venues.
santiago-de-compostela: Municipality in Galicia, Spain. In 1985, the city's Old Town was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
santiago: Capital and largest city of Chile. Most of the city lies between 500 and 650 meters (1,640 and 2,130 ft) above sea level, with recent urban growth extending into the Andean foothills.
santo-domingo: Capital and largest city of the Dominican Republic. Santo Domingo was founded in 1496 by the Spanish Empire and is the oldest continuously inhabited European settlement in the Americas.
santorini: Greek island in the Aegean Sea. It is the southernmost member of the Cyclades group of islands, with an area of approximately 73 km2 (28 mi2) and a 2021 census population of 15,480.
sao-paulo: Most populous city in Brazil. The city's name "São Paulo" honors Paul the Apostle and people from the capital city are known as paulistanos (while paulistas refers to people from the state of São Paulo more generally). The city's Latin motto is Non ducor, duco, which translates as "I am not led.
sao-tome: Capital and the largest city of São Tomé and Príncipe. Its name is Portuguese for "Saint Thomas". Founded in the 15th century, it is one of Africa's oldest colonial cities.
sapporo: City in Hokkaido, Japan. As of August 1, 2026, the city has a population of 1,962,596, making it the largest city in Hokkaido and the largest north of Tokyo.
sarajevo: Capital and largest city of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Sarajevo Canton, containing the city of Sarajevo and nearby municipalities, is home to 413,593 inhabitants.
sardinia: Island in the Mediterranean and region of Italy. It is located 200 kilometres (110 nautical miles) west of the Italian Peninsula, 200 km (110 nmi) north of Tunisia, and 16.5 km (9 nmi) south of the French island of Corsica.
sargasso-sea: Region of the North Atlantic Ocean. It lies between 20° and 35° north and 40° and 70° west and is approximately 1,100 kilometres (600 nautical miles) wide by 3,200 km (1,750 nmi) long.
savannah: City in Georgia, United States. The city is the most populous in the Coastal Georgia region and the fifth-most populous in the state as a whole, with a population of 147,780 at the 2020 census and an estimated 149,440 in 2025.
schonbrunn-palace: Palace in Vienna, Austria. The 1,441-room Baroque palace is one of the most important architectural, cultural, and historic monuments in the country.
scramble-for-africa: 1870s–1914 European colonisation of Africa. The 1884–1885 Berlin Conference regulated European colonisation and trade in Africa, and is seen as emblematic of the "scramble". In the last quarter of the 19th century, there were considerable political rivalries between the European empires, which provided the impetus for the colonisation.
sea-of-japan: Marginal sea between Japan, Russia and Korea. Like the Mediterranean Sea, it has almost no tides due to its nearly complete enclosure from the Pacific Ocean.
seattle: City in Washington, United States. It is the 18th-most populous city in the United States with a population of 784,777 in 2025, while the Seattle metropolitan area at over 4.15 million residents is the 15th-most populous metropolitan area in the nation.
second-battle-of-el-alamein: Battle in the Western Desert Campaign of the Second World War. In October 1942 Lieutenant-General Bernard Montgomery, commander of Eighth Army, opened his offensive against the Axis forces.
seoul: Capital and largest city of South Korea. The broader Seoul Metropolitan Area, encompassing Seoul, Gyeonggi Province and Incheon, emerged as the world's sixth largest metropolitan economy in 2022, behind New York, Tokyo, Los Angeles, Paris, and London, and hosts more than half of South Korea's population.
september-11-attacks: 2001 terror attacks in the U.S.. The first two planes were flown into each of the Twin Towers at the World Trade Center in New York City, while the third plane crashed into the Pentagon, the headquarters of the United States Department of Defense, in Arlington County, Virginia.
serengeti-national-park: National park in Tanzania. The Serengeti is known for the largest annual animal migration in the world of over 1.5 million western white-bearded wildebeest and 250,000 Grant's zebra, along with between 400-500,000 Thomson's gazelle and smaller herds of common eland.
seville: Capital of Andalusia and the Province of Seville, Spain. Seville has a municipal population of about 686,742 as of 2024, and a metropolitan population of about 1.5 million, making it the largest city in Andalusia and the 5th-largest city in Spain.
shanghai: Municipality and largest city in China. It has a population of 30,050,000 in the urban area as of 2026, thus making it China's most populous city and more broadly the fifth-largest city in the world by population.
sharpeville-massacre: 1960 South African Police killing of protestors. For more than fifty years the number of people killed and injured has been based on the police record, which included 249 victims in total, including 29 children, with 69 people killed and 180 injured.
sheffield: City in South Yorkshire, England. It is the second largest city in Yorkshire and the administrative centre of the larger metropolitan borough of Sheffield, which had an estimated population of 582,493 in 2024.
shenzhen: City in Guangdong, China. With a population of 18.2 million in 2025, Shenzhen is the third-most-populous city by urban population in China after Shanghai and Beijing.
shibuya-crossing: Scramble crossing in Tokyo. Inaugurated in 1973, the intersection is a popular tourist destination and a widely recognized symbol of the city of Tokyo through its frequent appearances in television, film, and other media.
shiraz: City in Fars province, Iran. As of the 2016 national census, the population of the city was 1,565,572 people, and its built-up area with Sadra was home to almost 1,800,000 inhabitants.
shwedagon-pagoda: Buddhist pagoda in Yangon, Myanmar. Built on the 51-metre-high (167 ft) Singuttara Hill, the 112 m (367 ft) tall pagoda stands 170 m (560 ft) above sea level, and dominates the Yangon skyline.
siberia: Geographical region of Russia comprising North Asia. It has formed a part of the sovereign territory of Russia and its predecessor states since the lengthy conquest of Siberia, which began with the fall of the Khanate of Sibir in 1582 and concluded with the annexation of Chukotka in 1778.
sicily: Island in the Mediterranean, region of Italy. Its most prominent landmark is Mount Etna, the tallest active volcano in Europe, and one of the most active in the world, currently 3,403 m (11,165 ft) high.
siege-of-acre: Part of the Crusades. The siege of Acre (also called the fall of Acre) took place in 1291 and resulted in the Crusaders' losing control of Acre to the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt.
siege-of-baghdad: Mongol conquest of the Abbasid Caliphate (1258). His massive army of over 138,000 men took years to reach the region but then quickly attacked and overpowered the Nizari Ismaili Assassins in 1256.
siege-of-jerusalem: Christian conquest of the First Crusade. The five-week siege began on 7 June 1099 and was carried out by the Christian forces of Western Europe mobilized by Pope Urban II after the Council of Clermont in 1095.
siege-of-leningrad: Blockade by the Axis powers, 1941–1944. Leningrad, the country's second largest city, was besieged by Germany and Finland for 872 days, but never captured.
siege-of-malta: Ottoman Empire's invasion of Malta in 1565. The Knights Hospitaller had been headquartered in Malta since 1530, after being driven out of Rhodes, also by the Ottomans, in 1522, following the siege of Rhodes.
siege-of-numantia: Siege of a Celtiberian city by the Roman Republic. The Numantine War was the third of the Celtiberian Wars and it broke out in 143 BC.
siege-of-sarajevo: Siege during the Bosnian War (1992–1996). Lasting from 5 April 1992 to 29 February 1996 (1,425 days), the siege was three times longer than the Battle of Stalingrad and more than a year longer than the siege of Leningrad, making it the longest siege of a capital city in the history of modern warfare.
siege-of-sevastopol: Part of the Crimean War. The Siege of Sevastopol (at the time called in English the Siege of Sebastopol) lasted from October 1854 until September 1855, during the Crimean War.
siege-of-vicksburg: Battle of the American Civil War. When two major assaults against the Confederate fortifications, on May 19 and 22, were repulsed with heavy casualties, Grant decided to besiege the city beginning on May 25.
siege-of-vienna: 1683 battle between the Christian European States and the Ottomans. In the ensuing war that lasted until 1699, the Holy Roman Empire consolidated territorial gains resulting in most of Ottoman Hungary being ceded to Leopold I, Holy Roman Emperor.
siege-of-yorktown: 1781 siege of the American Revolutionary War. The French and American armies united north of New York City during the summer of 1781.
siem-reap: Second-largest city in Cambodia. Siem Reap was named the ASEAN City of Culture for the period 2021–2022 at the 9th Meeting of the ASEAN Ministers Responsible for Culture and Arts (AMCA) organized on Oct 22, 2020.
sigiriya: Ancient rock fortress near Dambulla, Sri Lanka. Sigiriya today is a UNESCO listed World Heritage Site.
signing-of-the-magna-carta: English charter of freedoms made in 1215. Neither side stood by their commitments, and the charter was annulled by Pope Innocent III, leading to the First Barons' War.
singapore: Island country in Southeast Asia. During World War II, Singapore was occupied by Japan in 1942 and returned to Britain as a Crown colony following Japan's surrender in 1945.
sinking-of-the-titanic: 1912 maritime disaster. The largest ocean liner in service at the time, Titanic was four days into her maiden voyage from Southampton, England, to New York City, United States, with over 2,200 people on board when she struck an iceberg at 23:40 (ship's time) on 14 April.
six-day-war: 1967 war between Israel and Arab states. Military hostilities broke out amid poor relations between Israel and its Arab neighbors, who had been observing the 1949 Armistice Agreements signed at the end of the First Arab–Israeli War.
skopje: Capital and largest city of North Macedonia. The city — known as Scupi at the time — was founded in the late 1st century during the rule of Domitian, and abandoned in 518 after an earthquake destroyed the city.
sochi: City in Krasnodar Krai, Russia. The city covers an area of 176.77 square kilometers (68.25 sq mi), while the Greater Sochi Area covers over 3,502 square kilometers (1,352 sq mi). Sochi stretches across 145 kilometers (90 mi), and is the longest city in Europe (territorially).
sofia: Capital and largest city of Bulgaria. From 1530 to 1836, Sofia was the regional capital of Rumelia Eyalet, the Ottoman Empire's largest and most important province.
south-china-sea: Marginal sea of the Western Pacific Ocean. It is bounded in the north by South China, in the west by the Indochinese Peninsula, in the east by the islands of Taiwan and northwestern Philippines (mainly Luzon, Mindoro, and Palawan), and in the south by Borneo, eastern Sumatra, and the Bangka Belitung Islands.
south-tarawa: Island of the Republic of Kiribati. The South Tarawa population centre consists of all the small islets from Betio in the west to Bonriki and Tanaea in the north-east, connected by the South Tarawa main road, with an approximate population of 73,073 as of 2026.
southampton: City in Hampshire, England. Southampton had a population of 248,922 at the 2021 census, making it one of the most populous cities in southern England.
southern-ocean: Ocean around Antarctica. The expedition's multibeam sonar team identified the deepest point at 60° 28' 46"S, 025° 32' 32"W, with a depth of 7,434 metres (24,390 ft). The expedition leader and chief submersible pilot, Victor Vescovo, has proposed naming this deepest point the "Factorian Deep".
soweto-uprising: 1976 student-led anti-apartheid protests in South Africa. The uprising sparked unrest throughout South Africa, with 575 deaths from violence by the end of February 1977.
space-needle: Observation tower in Seattle, Washington, U.S.. Located at 400 Broad Street in the Lower Queen Anne neighborhood, it was built in the Seattle Center for the 1962 World's Fair, which drew more than 2.3 million visitors.
spanish-armada: Fleet sailing against England in 1588. The Spanish Armada (often known as Invincible Armada, or the Enterprise of England, Spanish: Grande y Felicísima Armada, lit. 'Great and Most Fortunate Navy') was a Spanish fleet that sailed from Lisbon in late May 1588, and was the largest engagement of the undeclared Anglo-Spanish War.
spanish-civil-war: 1936–1939 civil war in Spain. The Nationalists were initially led by a military junta, until General Francisco Franco was appointed supreme leader on 1 October 1936 of what he called the Spanish State.
sphinx: Limestone statue of a resting sphinx. The oldest known monumental sculpture in Egypt, the Sphinx is part of the Memphite Necropolis and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
split: City in Croatia. The city itself has a population of over 160,000, while the metropolitan area encompasses approximately 310,000 inhabitants.
srebrenica-massacre: 1995 genocidal killing of Bosniak men. The Srebrenica massacre, also known as the Srebrenica genocide, was the July 1995 genocidal killing of more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys in and around the town of Srebrenica during the Bosnian War.
st-george-s: Capital and largest city of Grenada. The town has witnessed an economic boom from 2014 to 2016, and also improved its tourism and various other sectors in 2022 while preserving its history, culture, and natural environment.
st-john-s: Capital and largest city of Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada. With a metropolitan population of approximately 239,316 (as of 16 January 2025), the St. John's Metropolitan Area is Canada's 22nd-largest metropolitan area and the second-largest Census Metropolitan Area (CMA) in Atlantic Canada, after Halifax, Nova Scotia.
st-paul-s-cathedral: Anglican cathedral in London, England. At 365 ft (111 m) high, it was the tallest building in London from 1710 to 1963.
st-peter-s-basilica: Roman Catholic basilica and landmark in Vatican City. Designed principally by Donato Bramante, Michelangelo, and Carlo Maderno, with piazza and fittings by Gian Lorenzo Bernini, Saint Peter's is one of the most renowned works of Italian Renaissance architecture and is the largest church in the world by interior measure.
statue-of-liberty: Colossal sculpture in New York Harbor. In 1865, the French historian and abolitionist Édouard de Laboulaye proposed a monument to commemorate the upcoming centennial of U.S. independence (1876), the perseverance of American democracy and the liberation of the nation's slaves.
stavanger: City in Rogaland, Norway. It is the third largest city and third largest metropolitan area in Norway (through conurbation with neighboring Sandnes Municipality) and the administrative center of Rogaland county.
stockholm: Capital and most populous city of Sweden. The area has been settled since the Stone Age, in the 6th millennium BC, and was founded as a city in 1252 by Swedish statesman Birger Jarl.
stonehenge: Prehistoric monument in England. The stones are set within earthworks in the middle of the densest complex of Neolithic and Bronze Age monuments in England, including several hundred tumuli (burial mounds). Stonehenge was constructed in several phases, beginning about 3100 BC and continuing until about 1600 BC.
storming-of-the-bastille: Major event of the French Revolution. In France, 14 July is a national holiday called Fête nationale française which commemorates both the anniversary of the storming of the Bastille and the Fête de la Fédération which occurred on its first anniversary in 1790.
strait-of-gibraltar: Strait connecting the Atlantic to the Mediterranean. The Strait's depth ranges between 300 and 900 metres (980 and 2,950 feet; 160 and 490 fathoms). The strait lies in the territorial waters of Morocco, Spain, and the British overseas territory of Gibraltar.
strait-of-malacca: Strait between the Malay Peninsula and the Indonesian island of Sumatra. The Strait of Malacca is a narrow stretch of water, 900 kilometres (560 mi) long and from 65 to 250 km (40 to 155 mi) wide, between the Malay Peninsula to the northeast and the Indonesian island of Sumatra to the southwest.
strasbourg: Prefecture in Grand Est, France. Strasbourg's metropolitan area had a population of 875,163 the same year, making it the eighth-largest metro area in France and home to 14% of the Grand Est region's inhabitants.
stuttgart: Capital of Baden-Württemberg, Germany. Stuttgart has a population of 613,111 as of 2023, making it the sixth largest city in Germany, while over 2.8 million people live in the city's administrative region and nearly 5.5 million people live in its metropolitan area, making it the fourth largest metropolitan area in Germany.
sucre: Capital city in Chuquisaca Department, Bolivia. Located in the south-central part of the country, Sucre lies at an elevation of 2,790 m (9,150 ft), making it the second-highest capital city in the world after Quito.
suez-canal: Artificial sea-level waterway in Egypt. Construction of the canal lasted from 1859 to 1869 and it officially opened on 17 November 1869.
suez-crisis: 1956 British–French–Israeli invasion of Egypt. Israel's four-month-long occupation of the Egyptian-occupied Gaza Strip and Egypt's Sinai Peninsula enabled it to attain freedom of navigation through the Straits of Tiran, but the Suez Canal was closed from October 1956 to March 1957.
sugarloaf-mountain: Peak in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. This became part of a World Heritage Site declared by UNESCO in 2012.
summer-palace: Complex of gardens and palaces in Beijing, China; UNESCO World Heritage Site. In December 1998, UNESCO included the Summer Palace on its World Heritage List.
surabaya: Capital and largest city of East Java, Indonesia. With 3,003,860 people living in the city as of mid 2025 (comprising 1,487,077 males and 1,516,783 females) and over 10 million in the extended Surabaya metropolitan area, according to the latest official estimate, Surabaya is the second-largest metropolitan area in Indonesia.
sutherland-falls: Waterfall in New Zealand. At 580 metres (1,904 feet) the falls are among the tallest waterfall in New Zealand.
suva: Capital and largest city of Fiji. The metropolitan population of Suva including the towns of Lami, Nasinu, and Nausori was 268,423 (this urban complex, excluding Lami, is also known as the Suva-Nausori corridor). Suva is Fiji's political, economic, and cultural centre.
svalbard: Norwegian archipelago in the Arctic Ocean. The largest island is Spitsbergen (37,673 km2), followed in size by Nordaustlandet (14,443 km2), Edgeøya (5,073 km2), and Barentsøya (1,288 km2). Bjørnøya or Bear Island (178 km2) is the most southerly island in the territory, situated some 147 km south of Spitsbergen.
sydney-harbour-bridge: Bridge across Sydney Harbour in Australia. Under the direction of John Bradfield of the New South Wales Department of Public Works, the bridge was designed and built by British firm Dorman Long of Middlesbrough, and opened in 1932.
sydney-opera-house: Performing arts centre in Australia. Designed by Danish architect Jørn Utzon and completed by an Australian architectural team headed by Peter Hall, the building was formally opened by Queen Elizabeth II on 20 October 1973, 16 years after Utzon's 1957 selection as winner of an international design competition.
sydney: Capital city of New South Wales, Australia. In 1788, the First Fleet of convicts, led by Arthur Phillip, founded Sydney as a British penal colony, the first European settlement in Australia.
table-mountain: Mountain overlooking Cape Town, South Africa. The mountain has 2,285 plant species, of which around 80% are fynbos (Afrikaans for 'fine bush'). Table Mountain National Park is the most visited national park in South Africa, attracting 4.2 million people every year for various activities.
tabriz: City in East Azerbaijan, Iran. The city was named World Carpet Weaving City by the World Crafts Council in October 2015 and Exemplary Tourist City of 2018 by the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.
tahiti: Island in French Polynesia. Tahiti's population was 189,517 in 2017, making it by far the most populous island in French Polynesia and accounting for 68.7% of the collectivity's total population; the 2022 Census recorded a population of 191,779.
taipei: Capital city of Taiwan. The municipality of Taipei is home to an estimated population of 2,494,813 (March 2023), forming the core part of the Taipei–Keelung metropolitan area, also known as "Greater Taipei", which includes the nearby cities of New Taipei and Keelung with a population of 7,047,559.
taiping-rebellion: Major rebellion in China (1850–1864). The conflict lasted 14 years, from its outbreak in 1850 until the fall of Taiping-controlled Nanjing—which had been renamed to Tianjing ("heavenly capital")—in 1864.
taj-mahal: Marble mausoleum in Agra, India. It was commissioned in 1631 by the fifth Mughal emperor, Shah Jahan (r. 1628–1658), to house the tomb of his late wife, Mumtaz Mahal; it also houses the tomb of Shah Jahan himself.
tallinn: Capital and largest city of Estonia. Located on a bay in northern Estonia, on the shore of the Gulf of Finland of the Baltic Sea, it has a population of 452,563 as of 2026, making it the third most-populous city in the Baltics.
tampere: City in Western Finland. Tampere and its surroundings are part of the historic province of Satakunta, but the area belonged to the province of Häme (Tavastia) from 1831 to 1997 and it has often been considered part of that province.
tangier: City in and capital of Tanger-Tetouan-Al Hoceima, Morocco. That status came to an end with Moroccan independence, in phases between 1956 and 1960.
tashkent: Capital and largest city of Uzbekistan. It is the most populous city in Central Asia, with a population of more than 3.1 million people as of July 1, 2025.
tasman-sea: Marginal sea of the South Pacific between Australia and New Zealand. The sea was named after the Dutch explorer Abel Janszoon Tasman, who in 1642 was the first known European to cross it.
tbilisi: Capital and the largest city of Georgia (country). Between 1801 and 1917, then part of the Russian Empire, it was the seat of the Caucasus Viceroyalty, governing both the northern and southern sides of the Caucasus.
tegucigalpa: Capital and largest city of Honduras. Claimed on 29 September 1578 by the Spaniards, Tegucigalpa became the Honduran capital on 30 October 1880, under President Marco Aurelio Soto, when he moved the seat of government from Comayagua, which had been the Honduran capital since its independence in 1841.
tehran: Capital and largest city of Iran. With a population of around 9 million in the city, and 16.8 million in the metropolitan area, Tehran is the most populous city in Iran and West Asia, the largest metropolitan area in the Middle East and the 24th-most-populous metropolitan area in the world.
tel-aviv: City in Central Israel. Tel Aviv is home to Tel Aviv University, the largest university in the country with more than 30,000 students.
temple-of-heaven: Imperial complex of religious buildings in Beijing, China. The Temple of Heaven was inscribed as a World Heritage site in 1998 and was described as "a masterpiece of architecture and landscape design which simply and graphically illustrates a cosmogony of great importance for the evolution of one of the world's great civilizations..." as the "symbolic.
teotihuacan: Ancient Mesoamerican city. At its zenith, perhaps in the first half of the first millennium (1 CE to 500 CE), Teotihuacan was the largest city in the Americas.
terracotta-army: Collection of ancient Chinese military statues. Estimates from 2007 were that the three pits containing the Terracotta Army hold more than 8,000 soldiers, 130 chariots with 520 horses, and 150 cavalry horses, the majority of which remain in situ.
tet-offensive: 1968 Vietnam War military campaign. The name is the truncated version of the Lunar New Year festival name in Vietnamese, Tết Nguyên Đán, a holiday period when most ARVN personnel were on leave.
the-hague: City and municipality in the Netherlands. The Hague is the core municipality of the Greater The Hague urban area containing over 800,000 residents, and is also part of the Rotterdam–The Hague metropolitan area, which, with a population of approximately 2.6 million, is the largest metropolitan area of the Netherlands.
the-little-mermaid: Sculpture by Edvard Eriksen. It is 1.25 metres (4.1 ft) tall and weighs 175 kilograms (385 lb). Based on the 1837 fairy tale of the same name by Danish author Hans Christian Andersen, the small and unimposing statue is a Copenhagen icon and has been a major tourist attraction since its unveiling in 1913.
thessaloniki: Second-largest city in Greece. It is the largest city of Northern Greece, with over 300,000 in the city proper and slightly over one million inhabitants in its metropolitan area, the capital of the geographic region of Macedonia, and the Decentralized Administration of Macedonia and Thrace.
thimphu: Capital and largest city of Bhutan. The ancient capital city of Punakha was replaced by Thimphu as the capital in 1955, and in 1961 Thimphu was officially declared the capital of the Kingdom of Bhutan by the 3rd Druk Gyalpo Jigme Dorji Wangchuck.
tiananmen-square-protests-of-1989: Student-led demonstrations in China. The events are sometimes called the '89 Democracy Movement, the Tiananmen Square Incident, or the Tiananmen uprising.
tijuana: Largest city in Baja California, Mexico. The international metropolitan region including San Diego was estimated at 5,158,459 in 2016, making it the third-largest metropolitan area in the Californias, 19th-largest metropolitan area in the Americas, and the largest bi-national conurbation that is shared between the US and Mexico.
tikal: Ruins of major ancient Maya city. The site is part of Guatemala's Tikal National Park, which was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979.
timbuktu: City in Tombouctou Region, Mali. In the first half of the 15th century, the Tuareg people took control for a short period, until the expanding Songhai Empire absorbed it in 1468.
times-square: Intersection and area in Manhattan, New York. Approximately 330,000 people pass through Times Square daily, many of them tourists, while over 460,000 pedestrians walk through Times Square on its busiest days.
tirana: Capital city of Albania. Tirana was founded in 1614 by Ottoman Albanian nobleman Sylejman Pasha Bargjini, centered on the Old Mosque and türbe.
tokyo-skytree: Broadcasting and observation tower in Japan. It has been the tallest tower in Japan since opening in 2012, and reached its full height of 634 metres (2,080 feet) in early 2011, making it the tallest tower in the world, displacing the Canton Tower.
tokyo-tower: Communications and observation tower in Japan. At 332.9 meters (1,092 feet), it was the tallest tower in Japan until the construction of Tokyo Skytree in 2012.
tokyo: Capital and most populous city in Japan. The Greater Tokyo Area, which includes Tokyo and parts of six neighboring prefectures, is the third-most populous metropolitan area in the world, with 33 million residents as of 2025.
toledo: City in Castilla–La Mancha, Spain. Built on a previous Carpetanian settlement, Toledo developed into an important Roman city of Hispania, later becoming the capital of the Visigothic Kingdom and seat of a powerful archdiocese.
toronto: Most populous city in Canada. The city is the fourth-most populous city in North America, behind Mexico City, New York City, and Los Angeles, with a census population of 2,794,356 as of 2021.
torres-del-paine: Mountain group in Torres del Paine, Chile. It is 280 km (170 mi) north of Punta Arenas, and about 1,960 km (1,220 mi) south of the Chilean capital Santiago.
torshavn: Capital and largest city of the Faroe Islands. To the northwest of the city lies the 347-meter-high (1,138 ft) mountain Húsareyn, and to the southwest, the 350-meter-high (1,150 ft) Kirkjubøreyn.
toulouse: Prefecture and commune in France. It is the fourth-largest city in France after Paris, Marseille, and Lyon, with 514,819 inhabitants within its municipal boundaries (2023); its metropolitan area has a population of 1,529,112 inhabitants (2023). Toulouse is the central city of one of the 22 metropolitan councils of France.
tower-bridge: Bridge over the Thames in London, England. Tower Bridge is a Grade I listed combined bascule, suspension, and, until 1960, cantilever bridge in London, built between 1886 and 1894, designed by Horace Jones and engineered by John Wolfe Barry with the help of Henry Marc Brunel.
tower-of-london: Castle in London, England. The White Tower, which gives the castle its name, was built by William the Conqueror in 1078 and was initially a resented symbol of oppression.
trans-siberian-railway: Railway network spanning Russia. During the period of the Russian Empire, government ministers—personally appointed by Alexander III and his son Nicholas II—supervised the building of the railway network between 1891 and 1916.
treaty-of-versailles: One of the treaties that ended World War I. As the most important treaty of World War I, it ended the state of war between Germany and most of the Allied Powers.
trevi-fountain: Fountain in Rome, Italy. Standing 26.3 metres (86 ft) high and 49.15 metres (161.3 ft) wide, it is the largest Baroque fountain in the world and one of the most famous fountains in the world.
trinity: First detonation of a nuclear weapon. The test was of an implosion-design plutonium bomb, or "gadget" – the same design as the Fat Man bomb later detonated over Nagasaki, Japan, on August 9, 1945.
tripoli: Capital and most populous city of Libya. It includes the port of Tripoli and the country's largest commercial and manufacturing center.
troms: Town in Tromsø Municipality, Norway. The 13.8-square-kilometre (3,400-acre) town has a population (2024) of 42,782 and a population density of 3,100 inhabitants per square kilometre (8,000/sq mi). In 2026, Tromsø holds the title of European Youth Capital, becoming the northernmost city to ever receive this designation.
trondheim: City in Norway. The settlement was founded in 997 as a trading post and served as the capital of Norway through the Viking Age until 1217.
trujillo: City in La Libertad, Peru. It is the third most populous city and center of the third most populous metropolitan area of Peru.
tulum: Maya site in Quintana Roo, Mexico. The ruins are situated on 12-meter-tall (39 ft) cliffs along the east coast of the Yucatán Peninsula on the Caribbean Sea.
tunis: Capital and largest city of Tunisia. As of 2020, it was the third-largest city in the Maghreb region (after Casablanca and Algiers) and the fifteenth-largest in the Arab world.
turin: City in Piedmont, Italy. From 1861 to 1865, it was the first capital of the Kingdom of Italy.
turku: City in southwest Finland. It is the 6th–most populous municipality in Finland, and the third–most populous urban area in the country after Helsinki and Tampere.
ulaanbaatar: Capital and largest city of Mongolia. The city was founded in 1639 as a nomadic Buddhist monastic centre, changing location 29 times, and was permanently settled at its modern location in 1778.
uluru: Sandstone monolith in the Northern Territory, Australia. It crops out near the centre of Australia in the southern part of the Northern Territory, 335 km (208 mi) south-west of Alice Springs.
united-states-capitol: Meeting place of the United States Congress. Central sections of the present building were completed in 1800, when the 6th U.S. Congress convened there on November 17, 1800, moving the national capital from Philadelphia to Washington, D.C.. The building was partly destroyed in the 1814 Burning of Washington by British forces.
united-states-declaration-of-independenc: 1776 American national founding document. On July 4, 1776, it was adopted unanimously by the Second Continental Congress, who were convened at the Pennsylvania State House, later renamed Independence Hall, in Philadelphia.
universal-studios-hollywood: Film studio and theme park in the US. Owned by NBCUniversal (Comcast) and operated by Universal Destinations & Experiences, it is one of the oldest and most famous Hollywood film studios still in use.
uppsala: City in Uppland, Sweden. Founded in 1477, Uppsala University is the oldest centre of higher education in Scandinavia.
ushuaia: City and port in Tierra del Fuego, Argentina. It is the only municipality in the Department of Ushuaia and has an area of 9,390 km2 (3,625 sq mi). It was founded on 12 October 1884 by Augusto Lasserre and is located on the shores of the Beagle Channel surrounded by the mountain range of the Martial Glacier, in the Bay of Ushuaia.
utrecht: City and municipality in Utrecht, Netherlands. It has a population of 378,140 as of January 2026.
uxmal: Ancient Maya city. It is considered one of the most important archaeological sites of Maya culture, along with Palenque, Chichen Itza and Calakmul in Mexico, Caracol and Xunantunich in Belize, and Tikal in Guatemala.
vaduz: Capital of Liechtenstein. Although Vaduz is the best-known town in the principality internationally, it is not the largest; neighbouring Schaan has a larger population.
valencia: Municipality in Spain. With a population of 824,340, it is the third most-populous city in Spain.
valletta: Capital of Malta. It is also the southernmost capital of Europe, and, at just 0.61 square kilometres (0.24 sq mi), it is the European Union's second-smallest capital city.
valley-of-the-kings: Necropolis in ancient Egypt. With the 2005 discovery of a new chamber and the 2008 discovery of two further tomb entrances, the Valley of the Kings is known to contain 65 tombs and chambers, ranging in size from the simple pit that is KV54 to the complex tomb that is KV5.
valparaiso: Second largest city in Chile. Valparaiso is the second-largest city in the metro area (behind Viña del Mar). It is located about 120 km (75 mi) northwest of Santiago, by road, and is one of the Pacific Ocean's most important seaports.
vancouver: City in British Columbia, Canada. As the most populous city in the province, the 2021 Canadian census recorded 662,248 people in the city, up from 631,486 in 2016.
varanasi: Metropolis in Uttar Pradesh, India. It is 692 kilometres (430 mi) to the southeast of India's capital New Delhi and 320 kilometres (200 mi) to the southeast of the state capital, Lucknow.
vatican-city: Enclaved Holy See's independent city-state. The independent state of Vatican City came into existence in 1929 via the Lateran Treaty between the Holy See and the Kingdom of Italy, which spoke of it as a creation, not as a vestige of the much larger Papal States (756–1870), which had previously encompassed much of Central Italy.
venice: City in Veneto, Italy. The islands are in the shallow Venetian Lagoon, an enclosed bay lying between the mouths of the Po and the Piave rivers (more exactly between the Brenta and the Sile). As of 2026, the city proper (municipality of Venice) has a population of 249,385.
verona: City in Veneto, Italy. The metropolitan area of Verona covers an area of 1,426 km2 (550.58 sq mi) and has a population of 714,310 inhabitants.
victoria-falls: Waterfall on the Zambezi River in Zambia and Zimbabwe. Although known to some European geographers before the 19th century, Scottish missionary David Livingstone was introduced to the falls in 1855, naming them Victoria Falls after Queen Victoria.
victoria: Capital city of Seychelles. In 2022, the Central region, comprising nine administrative districts within and around the capital, accounted for 30,145 (~30%) of the country's total population of 102,612.
vienna: Capital and largest city of Austria. Vienna is the cultural, economic, and political centre of the country, the fifth-largest city by population in the European Union, and the most populous of the cities on the river Danube.
vientiane: Capital of Laos. The city had a population of 840,000 as of the 2023 census.
vilnius: Capital and largest city of Lithuania. The city was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1994.
vinson-massif: Largest mountain in Antarctica. Mount Vinson is the highest peak in Antarctica, at 4,892 meters (16,050 ft). It lies in the north part of Vinson Massif's summit plateau in the south portion of the main ridge of the Sentinel Range about 2 kilometers (1+1⁄4 mi) north of Hollister Peak.
vladivostok: Largest city and administrative center of Primorsky Krai, Russia. It is located around the Golden Horn Bay on the Sea of Japan, covering an area of 331.16 square kilometers (127.86 square miles), with a population of 603,519 residents as of 2021.
voyages-of-christopher-columbus: 1492–1504 voyages to the Americas. These voyages led to Europeans learning about the New World and were an early breakthrough in the period known in Europe as the Age of Exploration, which saw the colonization of the Americas, a related biological exchange, and the beginning of trans-Atlantic trade.
wadi-rum: Valley in southern Jordan. The Wadi Rum Protected Area has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2011.
walt-disney-world: Entertainment resort in Orlando, Florida, US. Opened on October 1, 1971, the resort is operated by Disney Experiences, a division of the Walt Disney Company.
warsaw: Capital and largest city of Poland. Its population is officially estimated at 1.87 million residents within a greater metropolitan area of around 3.5 million residents, which makes Warsaw the 7th most populous city in the European Union.
washington-monument: U.S. national memorial in Washington, D.C.. The Washington Monument is a 555-foot (169 m) tall obelisk on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., built to commemorate George Washington, a Founding Father of the United States and the nation's first president.
washington: Federal capital district of the United States. Washington, D.C., officially the District of Columbia and commonly known as Washington, is the federal capital city of the United States, and its only federal district.
wat-arun: Buddhist temple in central Bangkok, Thailand. Built with a fusion of Indian influences, incorporating elements of both Hindu and Buddhist symbolism, as well as reflecting Siamese tradition and identity.
wellington: Capital city of New Zealand. The Wellington urban area, which only includes urbanised areas within Wellington City, has a population of 209,800 as of June 2025.
westminster-abbey: Church in London, England. The monastery was dissolved in 1559, and the church was made a royal peculiar – a Church of England church, accountable directly to the sovereign – by Elizabeth I. The abbey.
white-house: Residence and workplace of the US president. Reconstruction began almost immediately, and President James Monroe moved into the partially reconstructed Executive Residence in October 1817.
whitehorse: Capital and largest city of Yukon, Canada. It was incorporated in 1950 and is located at kilometre 1426 (Historic Mile 918) on the Alaska Highway in southern Yukon.
willis-tower: Skyscraper in Chicago, Illinois. The Willis Tower, formerly known and still commonly referred to as the Sears Tower, is a 110-story, 1,451-foot (442.3 m) skyscraper in the Loop of Chicago, Illinois, United States.
windhoek: Capital and largest city of Namibia. It is located in central Namibia on the Khomas Highland plateau area, at around 1,700 m (5,600 ft) above sea level in the geographical centre of the country.
windsor-castle: Official country residence of British monarch. Since the time of Henry I (who reigned 1100–1135), it has been used by the monarch and is the longest-occupied palace in Europe.
winnipeg: Capital city of Manitoba, Canada. As of 2021, Winnipeg had a city population of 749,607 and a metropolitan population of 834,678, making it Canada's sixth-largest city and eighth-largest metropolitan area.
woodstock: 1969 music festival in Bethel, New York, US. The Woodstock Music and Art Fair, commonly referred to as Woodstock, was a music festival held from August 15 to 18, 1969, on Max Yasgur's dairy farm in Bethel, New York, 60 miles (95 km) southwest of the town of Woodstock.
wright-brothers: American aviation pioneers, inventors of the airplane. In 1904 the Wright brothers developed the Wright Flyer II, which made longer-duration flights including the first circle, followed in 1905 by the first truly practical fixed-wing aircraft, the Wright Flyer III.
wrigley-field: Baseball stadium in Chicago, Illinois, US. It first opened in 1914 as Weeghman Park for Charles Weeghman's Chicago Whales of the Federal League, which folded after the 1915 baseball season.
wroc-aw: Historical capital and largest city of Silesia, located in southwestern Poland. In 2025, the official population of Wrocław was 672,545, making it the third-largest city in Poland.
xi-an: Capital and largest city of Shaanxi, China. A sub-provincial city on the Guanzhong plain, the city is the most populous in the province and third-most populous in Western China after Chongqing and Chengdu, as well as the most populous in Northwestern China.
yalta-conference: 1945 WWII allied discussion of postwar reorganization. It was preceded by the Tehran Conference in November 1943 and was followed by the Potsdam Conference in July 1945.
yamoussoukro: Capital city of Ivory Coast. As of the 2014 census, Yamoussoukro is the third most populous city in the Ivory Coast, with a population of 361,893.
yangon: Largest city of Myanmar. The city is also home to the gilded Shwedagon Pagoda – Myanmar's most sacred and famous Buddhist pagoda.
yaounde: Capital of Cameroon. The outpost of Epsumb or Jeundo was founded between the Nyong and Sanaga rivers at the northern edge of the area's forests in 1887 by German explorers as a trading base for rubber and ivory.
yaren: District and de facto capital of Nauru. Yaren (formerly known as Makwa and Moqua) is a district of the Pacific island country of Nauru, officially the Republic of Naoero.
yekaterinburg: City in Sverdlovsk Oblast, Russia. Yekaterinburg is the fourth most populous city in Russia, the largest city in the Ural Federal District, and one of Russia's main cultural and industrial centres.
yellowstone-national-park: National park in the western United States. The park is known for its wildlife and its many geothermal features, especially the Old Faithful geyser, one of its most popular.
yerevan: Capital and largest city of Armenia. The city also serves as the seat of the Araratian Pontifical Diocese, which is the largest diocese of the Armenian Apostolic Church and one of the oldest dioceses in the world.
yom-kippur-war: 1973 war between Israel and Arab states. Most of the fighting occurred in the Sinai Peninsula and the Golan Heights, territories occupied by Israel in 1967.
york: City in North Yorkshire, England. York's built-up area had a recorded population of 141,685 at the 2021 census.
yosemite-national-park: National park in California, United States. Designated a World Heritage Site in 1984, Yosemite is internationally recognized for its granite cliffs, waterfalls, clear streams, groves of giant sequoia, lakes, mountains, meadows, glaciers, and biological diversity.
zagreb: Capital city and county in Croatia. At the 2021 census, the city itself had a population of 767,131, while the population of the Zagreb metropolitan area is 1,086,528.
zanzibar-city: District of Mjini Magharibi Region, Tanzania. Stone Town is the historical core of the city, the former capital of the Zanzibar Sultanate; because of its unique architecture and culture, it was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000.
zanzibar: Semi-autonomous region of Tanzania. Including the Mafia Archipelago, the Zanzibar Archipelago is sometimes referred to locally as the "Spice Islands". Tourism in Zanzibar is a more recent activity, driven by government promotion that caused an increase from 19,000 tourists in 1985 to 376,000 in 2016 and 917,000 in 2025.
zaragoza: Capital of Aragon, Spain. As of 2025, Zaragoza had a population of 699,007 inhabitants, making it the fourth most populous in Spain, on a land area of 973.78 square kilometres (375.98 square miles) and is the centre of a metropolitan area of around 0.76 million.
zhangjiajie-national-forest-park: National forest in Hunan, China. It is one of several national parks within the Wulingyuan Scenic Area.
zion-national-park: National park in Utah, United States. The lowest point in the park is 3,666 ft (1,117 m) at Coalpits Wash and the highest peak is 8,726 ft (2,660 m) at Horse Ranch Mountain.
zocalo: Plaza de la Constitución, Mexico City. Even so, it is almost always called the Zócalo today.

2023-turkey-syria-earthquakes: On 6 February 2023, two earthquakes devastated southern and central Turkey and northern and western Syria.
battle-of-badr: The Battle of Badr or sometimes called The Raid of Badr (Arabic: غَزْوَةُ بَدْرٍ [ɣazwatu badr]; Ghazwatu Badr), also referred to as The Day of the Criterion (Arabic: يَوْمُ الْفُرْقَانْ.
neolithic-revolution: transition from hunter gatherer to settled peoples
ramsar-convention: The Ramsar Convention on Wetlands of International Importance Especially as Waterfowl Habitat is an international treaty for the conservation and sustainable use of Ramsar sites (wetlands).
april-2015-nepal-earthquake: The April 2015 Nepal earthquake (also known as the Gorkha earthquake) killed 8,962 people and injured 21,952 across the countries of Nepal, India, China and Bangladesh.
treaty-of-shimonoseki: treaty signed at the Shunpanrō hall, Shimonoseki, Japan on April 17, 1895, between the Empire of Japan and the Qing Empire, ending the First Sino-Japanese War.
battle-of-the-trench: failed besieging of early Muslims by Arab and Jewish forces in 627 CE
2008-sichuan-earthquake: An earthquake occurred in the province of Sichuan, China at 14:28:01 China Standard Time on May 12, 2008.
surrender-of-japan: The surrender of the Empire of Japan in World War II was announced by Emperor Hirohito on 15 August and formally signed on 2 September 1945, ending the war.
battle-of-issus: The Battle of Issus (also Issos) occurred in southern Anatolia, on 5 November 333 BC between the Hellenic League led by Alexander the Great and the Achaemenid (or Persian) Empire, led by Darius III.
2005-kashmir-earthquake: On 8 October 2005, at 08:50:39 PKT, a Mw 7.6 earthquake struck the Azad Kashmir region in northern Pakistan. Its epicenter was located in the tehsil of Patikka, near the city of Muzaffarabad.
rose-revolution: The Rose Revolution or Revolution of Roses (Georgian: ვარდების რევოლუცია, romanized: vardebis revolutsia) was a nonviolent change of power that occurred in Georgia in November 2003.
fall-of-kabul-2021: On 15 August 2021, Afghanistan's capital city of Kabul was captured by the Taliban after a major insurgent offensive that began in May 2021.
philippine-revolution: The Philippine Revolution was a war of independence waged by the revolutionary organization Katipunan against the Spanish Empire from 1896 to 1898.
indonesian-national-revolution: armed conflict and diplomatic struggle between Indonesia and the Dutch Empire
fall-of-singapore: Singapore was captured from the British by the Empire of Japan in February 1942 during the Second World War.
siege-of-jerusalem-1187: The siege of Jerusalem lasted from 20 September to 2 October 1187, when Balian of Ibelin surrendered the city to the forces of the Ayyubid Sultanate under sultan Saladin.
siege-of-jerusalem-70-ce: The siege of Jerusalem in 70 CE was the decisive event of the First Jewish Revolt against the Roman Empire (66–73 CE).
1999-izmit-earthquake: An earthquake of moment magnitude 7.6 struck Kocaeli Province, Turkey, on 17 August 1999.
siege-of-antioch: The siege of Antioch took place during the First Crusade in 1097 and 1098, on the Crusaders' way to Jerusalem through Syria. Two sieges took place in succession.
2018-sulawesi-earthquake-and-tsunami: On 28 September 2018, a shallow, large earthquake struck in the neck of the Minahasa Peninsula, Indonesia, with its epicentre located in the mountainous Donggala Regency, Central Sulawesi.
constitutionalization-attempts-in-iran: The Iranian Constitutional Revolution was a short-lived push for democratic rule in the form of a constitutional monarchy within a highly elitist yet decentralized society under the Qajars.
siege-of-tyre-332-bc: The siege of Tyre was carried out by Alexander the Great in 332 BC during his campaigns against the Persians.
siege-of-acre-1189-1191: The siege of Acre was the first significant counterattack by Guy of Jerusalem against Saladin, Sultan of Egypt and Syria.
libyan-civil-war-2011: 2011 armed conflict in the North African country of Libya
2023-al-haouz-earthquake: On 8 September 2023 at 23:11 DST (22:11 UTC), an earthquake with a moment magnitude of 6.9 and maximum Mercalli intensity of IX (Violent) struck Morocco's Al Haouz Province.
eighth-crusade: The Eighth Crusade was the second Crusade launched by Louis IX of France, this one against the Hafsid dynasty in Tunisia in 1270.
egyptian-revolution-of-1952: On 23 July 1952, a coup began in Egypt with the toppling of King Farouk in a coup d'état by the Free Officers Movement, a group of army officers led by Mohamed Naguib and Gamal Abdel Nasser.
battle-of-the-nile: The Battle of the Nile (also known as the Battle of Aboukir Bay; French: Bataille d'Aboukir) was fought between the Royal Navy and the French Navy at Aboukir Bay in Egypt between 1 and 3 August 1798.
battle-of-the-pyramids: The Battle of the Pyramids (French: Bataille des Pyramides), also known as the Battle of Embabeh (bataille d'Embabech), was fought on 21 July 1798 during the French invasion of Egypt and Syria.
siege-of-tobruk: The siege of Tobruk took place between 10 April and 27 November 1941, during the Western Desert campaign (1940–1943) of the Second World War.
1960-agadir-earthquake: The 1960 Agadir earthquake occurred on 29 February at 23:40:18 Western European Time near the city of Agadir, located in western Morocco on the shore of the Atlantic Ocean.
charter-of-the-united-nations: The Charter of the United Nations, also referred to as the UN Charter, is the foundational treaty of the United Nations.
american-revolution-q192769: The American Revolution (1765–1789) was a political movement in the Thirteen Colonies of Great Britain.
2010-chile-earthquake: On 27 February 2010 at 03:34 UTC−03:00, a Mww 8.8 megathrust earthquake struck off the coast of the Maule Region of central Chile.
2026-venezuela-earthquakes: On 24 June 2026, doublet large strike-slip earthquakes affected northwestern and central Venezuela.
may-revolution: The May Revolution (Spanish: Revolución de Mayo) was a week-long series of events that took place from 18 to 25 May 1810, in Buenos Aires, capital of the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata.
battle-of-the-river-plate: The Battle of the River Plate was fought in the South Atlantic on 13 December 1939 as the first British naval battle of the Second World War.
holi-q10259: Holi (IPA: ['hoːli:, hoːɭiː]) is a major Hindu festival of colours, love and spring. It celebrates the love between the deities Radha and Krishna.
mantra: Sacred utterance or sound used in meditation, often repeated
j-pop: J-pop (an abbreviated form of "Japanese popular music") is a form of popular music that entered the musical mainstream of Japan in the 1990s. In Japan it is known simply as pops (ポップス, poppusu).
noh: Noh (能, Nō; Japanese pronunciation: [no(ꜜ)ː], Sino-Japanese for "ability") is a major form of classical Japanese dance-drama that has been performed since the 14th century.
basbousa: semolina or farina cake soaked in simple syrup, it was invented in the 12-16 century
ugali: type of maize flour porridge made in Africa
homs: Homs (en árabe: حمص‎, Ḥimṣ) anteriormente conocida como Emesa (en griego: Ἔμεσα, Émesa),​ es la tercera ciudad más importante y poblada de Siria después de Damasco y Alepo.
